div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
(By Redcap.)
AN EGG.

What is an egg made up of? If more people anderatoed the real food value of an egg, more would be eaten. Analyzed, an egg consists of oxygen, hydregen, nitrogen and carbon. Eggs are very rich in Eitroonous-containing substances, and as cur bodies are largely made up of substances containing nitrogen we, by necessity, need food which conta‘ns that element in a large quantity, 'With the combination of other elements. I should ray that eggs are the moat nutritious of nitrogenous f, ode. Etr.Willoughby rays : Eggs are the s thy concentrated food known When couch pressed with work he says, "I find nothing better than a few eggs broken into milk and swallowed. In sustaining power in all dial goes to repair waste and supply fuel, they are as good as a big dinner." With these few and somewhat Ihnited remarks about the constituents of an egg, is it any wonder that the medical men of cur tune see in the egg mach value as a food diet. We have now what is known as

lIWWIT U. E.. WEEK. 11l include the copy of a letter received during the week the matter oil! explain itself. At the tame time! sincerely hope that some of my readers will help in this manner. A new laid egg on the break- fast table of a London hospital is a treat. And while the burden to sonic of us in sending a few eggs is not great, it will perhaes help to gladden the heart of a few poor invalids. 1 herefore if y.,n decide to do no, you will find all the instructions necessary in the Inflaming letter. "About this time last sear through the medium of your widely read columns—ever open in the cause of charity—we appealed to those of your readers who kept fowls to seed no any number of new laid eggs for the hospitals. We SUOMI ded, eilu your friendly help, in obtaining nearly 20,000 eggs, all of which were immediately distributed amotigst the various deserving Metropolitan hospitals. In the month of June, eggs are mist plentiful, and consequently keepers of laying fares will be well able to spare at least one dozen new !aids from their surplus. Them should he sent to me between the ' dates of June 7th nod June I dth earefully packed and carriage paid. All boxes vied 16,1 be returned on request. Special laLels for despatching epgs will be sent on application. Last year many letters from the benefitting hospitals were received, saying bow greatly these gifts were appreciated by the hospitals. The co-operation of the Hospital Saturday Fund has again been secured in the allocation of the gifts, aid it is earnestly hoped that all your readets who can send eggs will do no. They are sorely needed. All packages containing eggs will be rent direct to the Hospitals without being opened, no it is necessary that any covering let•er should le tlespatched separately. Ills also advisal le to state the number of eggs contained in each package on the outside of such comignment. Every gift of eggs soil be acki osledged by loins obedient servant, THE EDrroß. Daring the last stages of development before the chick emerges from the shell, it absorbs the whole of the yolk of the egg. Tlere is tot the least doubt that this forme the natural food sufficient to sustain the chick until it can " pick "for itself. Therefore it is quite safe to Pay that no food of al y depeription is needed for 21 to 30 hours. And when it is given before this period has elapsed, it is sheer unkindness to the chick itself as well as being uunecessary. Whilst dealing with this subject I urn reminded if an old breeder if game torch, and by-the-way a winner of more than one silver cup too. I paid him a viait on Easter Monday last. We wandered down his fields until we came to a hen- house right away from the farm. We mode a search of the sleeping quarters and found a hen with a nice little brood of 11 chickens. From all appermancei they had teen hatched out about 20 hones. They were easily nested in the bottom of a box about one foot deep on the floor of the sleeping quarters, which was about two fart fr m the ground floor. I asked my host when he intended feeding the chicks. His answer was :As soon as they are able to fly out of the box to look for some. 'ibis method, he added. I constantly adept. Well, readers, after all, practical experience is always the best teacher. And I agree with my friend that when his chicks were hungry, they e ould soon be out to look for food Hunger creates exertion and when burger is satisfied by a natural process nothing but good can follow as a consequence. Therefore I would urge that you should not be over anxious about "stuffing " the little mites until the system is absolutely clear of albumen. As soon as they start chirping loudly and emerging frequently hum under the hen, you may commeoce to feed them.

A good many chicks are lost, through want of thought and study of their natural habits. Professor A. Holloway says :—"The albumen f an egg is distinctly a stimulant. Half a tint of albumen water (white of an egg an water) is as stimulating as an ounce of brandy, and at the same time its food value is infinitely greater." So y 4 u see that by a clots* study of what the little creatures actually take into their systems, it is not neceresary to overload them with food in the early stages of their existence.

Every poultry farmer will now have chickens " We are right in the thick of it. We are being bit at with a spell of grand chicken-rearing seether. But because of this you should not take too mach advantage, think- ng that the loos of a few is not of much consequence. It is the best that die at times. Take every pecan- tion to rear every one possible. time them plenty of fresh air in the they-time,consisteot with some shading from the rays of the nun. If you have no natural ehadiog, erect a temporary one irl the form of a low roof made of a few thin boards; these are easily remnred later in the seas- n. They may took some- what unsightly, but if it means more comfort for the chicks and a gm it percentage reared, it will have paid you in the long run. Keep the drinking-water

fountains clean and renew as often as possible. Water which lies in the sun for long spells soon become. tainted. Keep a supply of chicken grit bandy and see that you give them perfect ventilation in the sleeping quarters. Avoid rigidly, coops with boarded doors; only this last week I have had to treat • 'bonnie ' Fever°lle chick for cramp— caused through sleeping in • dog kennel—if vou happen to haih them similarly effected you should treat them at once. Gat a small veesel full of hot water and mustard and bold the victims up to the hocks M the liquid for a fen. minutes. Repeat the process several times a day until improvement is noticeable. Eispeciallv during this fine weather the chicks will do equally well if housed en the hare earth. And when it is alnclotely necessary to use wood bottomed coops, then see that they are well covered si ith soil and prat-moss litter. The repetition cf those ch!cken hints is very necessary at this season of the year. So I weull ask you to pay special attention to every detail no that you may have a successful hatching Beason.

One ef my readers shou ed me a Jorge goose (gg this week, which had heed laid at a far m in Thelwall Notwithstanding the measurements (which were It inches long-ways acti S inches round) the egg was almost perfect shaped. The c Meats were emptied, and it was found to conbitt three distinct yolks. It would have been interesting if this egg had been incubated. The yolks were so distinct thet I feel sure that two geldings might hare been succe.sfully hatched out. however, it is too lore n ›w.

div.head: CRICKET, BOWLING, AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: CRICKET, BOWLING, AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket Notes

Victcry and defeat for the Warr ing,o‘iars have to Ire chronicled thi3 week. On Saturday Winningtm Park Nv ere entertained at Arpley and the home eleven had no difficulty in accounting for them, but on Monday Warriogton journeyed to Old Trafford and were handsomely beaten by Manchester. The match with Wilmington Patk lobed by no means a certainty for Warrington in the early stages, the visiting howlers making things decidedly urcomfortable for the wielders of the hut W. Richardson and J. P.". Bainbridge got will set aril added lii and 29 respectively, which put o decidedly better comnlesion on Warri,.gton's pro-pects. A. T. L. Orear and the Rev. llurace Gray also rrovieled a merry partnership and amas•ed DI and 11, while A. Duckworth carried out his I at with 12 to his credit, The home innings closed :or 116.

Winnington Perk were at Ills wickets fiffy-five minutes and nere all di.m7ssed for 1;3. J. Starker heading the score list with 33. Bennett blwled 11l great elfert and securtd the flan aus'ytis of six I wickets for 21 run...

On Monday Warrington took a dep'eted tram to Old Trafford, where they were pitted against no exceptionally strong aide. Manchester had first brook and runs came at a surprising pace, the inninas Icing declared at 262 for 7 a ickets. The bowling este repeatedly changed without result nod there were ands tall scores as F. Fairbanks 2. Whitehead's .Is, and R. W. Heyword's 50. The Warringtonians did not put up much of a fight and were sent to the rightabcut for 115, F. Stammer, (25) and J. Bain- bridge (27.3) beirg the chief contributors. Fairbank captured 4 wickets for 22 runs.

Warrington 2nd w, non time at Winnington Park, the finish being most exciting. Win, baton made n Flood start ard knocked up 80 for 3, but when 11. Hawthorn took up the bowling matters assumed a lens rose aspect for them and tho int,ings closed for 110. Ha; thorn bowled excellently and took five wickets for 20 runs. Guthrie batted in grand style for the home ' eleven, his total beirg .52. Warrington had their , work cut cut to secure the requieite number of runs in the specified time, but they forced matter with umnietakable energy and won c'everly by fire runs, with six wickets intact. S. Baster was in good form with the bat and made :13. W. V. Torten and It. Hawthorn played a prominent port in securing the victory, their partnership carrying the total from chase uFon 80 to 121. Torton carried out his but with 32 to his credit and Hawthorn 1111.1 bowled in the last over, having made a very useful 13.

div.p: EIFFEL TOWER LEMONADE
FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By PIOIIp Snowden, M.P. - TWO IMPORTANT INDUSTRIAL
REFORMS.

Last week two Bills of very great import- ance to the textile workers of the country were introduced into the House of Commons. One of these is a Government Bill, and it is understood that it is the intention of the Government to pass it into law this session. It is very doubtful if this intention will be realised in view of the very contentious nature of the measure and of the crowded state of the Government programme. The I other is a private member's Bill, and it has been brought forward more by way of advertisement than with any hope that it I will become law this year. I ABOLISHING THE HALF-TIMER. The Government Bill is a proposal to take I the drastic step of completely abolishing all half-time labour, and compelling the attend- ance of children at school up to the age of 14 years and in some cases up to 15. It is hardly possible to exaggerate the importance of this Bill in view of its effect on the great textile trades of the country, and especially in view of the hostility with which the proposal to raise the half-time age has always been regarded by the Lancashire cotton operatives. This Bill proposs to do much more than to raise the half-time age to 13 years. It gives power to the local Education authority to make by-laws under which a child may be compelled to go to school full time up to 15 years of age. Nobody can doubt the neces- sity for such a measure as this in the interests of education and the future welfare of the child, but it is such a drastic proposal that one doubts if the people who are going to be directly affected by the prohibition of child labour are yet prepared for such

it will be well to make as clear as possible what it is the Bill proposes to do. At present in England a child can go into a factory at 12 for half-time employment without any condition except that it must attend school the other half-day. At thirteen, if the child has attained a certain educational standard or has attended school a certain number of times within the previous five years, it may leave school altogether for full time employment. There is not in England at present any power to compel a child to attend an evening or continuation school after it has been exempted from day school attend- ance. In Scotland, under the last Education Act, the local authority can make by-laws enforcing attendance at a continuation school WHAT IS PROPOSED. It is proposed by this Bill (which by the , way does not touch Scotland or Ireland), that no child under any circumstances shall be allowed to go to work in a factory or in agriculture, or shall be exempted from school lattendance full time under the age of 13. No child shall be allowed to leave school at 13 except on very strict conditions. One ektep- tion is made in the case of a child going into employment in agriculture. But the educa- tion authority is not to grant a certificate of exemption for agricultural employment unless it is assured that the employment is likely to lead to employment of a permanent character. It is difficult to understand why the education laws should always go on the principle that a child intended for agricul- tural work need not be so well educated as one who is to go into a factory or workshop. But such is the idea.

For all other occupations the eobditions of exemption are very stringent. The child cannot leave school at 13 unless it under- takes to attend a continuation school for not less than 120 hours a year up to the age of 16. Not only is the child who leaves at 13 to be compelled to attend a continuation school up to sixteen years of age, but the local authority may make by-laws requiring all the children who leave at 14 or 15 to do so, but the hours of such attendance shall not exceed 150 in any twelve months. This is what this Bill proposes to do. It will be interesting to see what sort of a reception it gets from the parents of the children as a whole, and especially from the parents in the district where the half-time system is in operation. There has undoubtedly been a change in the opinion of Lancashire on the half-time question in recent years. The leaders of the trade unions are unanimously in favour of the gradual abolition of the system. They are convinced that half-time labour is neither beneficial nor economical. But the great majority of the operatives are opposed to any change. About two years ago a ballot of the Lancashire textile operatives was taken, and the result was : in favour of raising the age to thirteen, 34,120; against, 151,032. The question arises as to whether this change can be forced irto law in the face of the opposition of the parents concerned. This opposition is regrettable,but is the painful fact

div.head: 48 HOURS WEEK:
div.p: A 48 HOURS WEEK:

The other Bill to which I referred is one which has been introduced by the Labour members who represent the textile districts in Lancashire. It proposes to make a legal forty-eight hours week for the cotton trade. That this Bill should have been introduced by the leaders of the cotton operatives' trade unions and at the request of the organisation is a striking illustration of how opinion on this question has ripened in recent years. The frequent periods of short time have probably done much to convince the leaders of the unions that it is better to regulate the hours by a permanent weekly reduction. The Bill is ingeniously draft-A, and while in full sympathy with the object which is to secure a 48 hours week, I doubt if these details are the best which could be suggested. The Bill does not aim at an eight hours day, but a forty eight hours week, which are not the same things. It is important to limit the number of weekly hours of labour, but I think from every point of view it is better to do this by limiting the number of the daily hours. The Bill proposes to take three years to bring down the hours to 48 per week. The first year the hours are to be reduced by 2!, the next year by another 11 and the third year by 3'. hours. The reduction the first year is to be taken on the Monday morning, the factory not being allowed to start until nine o'clock in the morning. The second year the reduction is to be taken from the Tuesday morning, the starting time being nine o'clock. When the 48 hours week comes into operation, all Saturday is to be a holiday, and work is to started at 8.30 on Monday. I have backed the Bill as one in hearty sympathy with the proposal to reduce hours in the cotton trade. but I certainly do not think the arrangement of hours is at all satisfactory. To. begin work at nine a.m, is too late, especially in summer. It would be much better in my opinion to begin earlier and to get the reduc- tion at the other end. A LATER START.
I do not think it is a good thing to over- load the five days of the week in order to get la full day off on Saturday. This will mean that on the five days a week the hours will

be practically as long as they are at present The thing at which, in my opinion, those ought to aim who are seeking to reduce fa7tory hours is to avoid having to start at the unearthly hour of six in the morning or thereabouts. The working time before break- fast is not profitable. It could be abolished with advantage toeverybody concerned. . . . .
Another important .Matter from the point

iof view of experience n regard to economy of production is that the short working day for every day is better than a long regular day with an occasional complete holiday. The week-end holiday is very necessary, hut it is in no sense a compensation for five long days. The worker wants more leisure every day; it is not good to crowd the rest into one or two days, because then these holidays are nothing more than making up the exhausted vitality too long con tinuous.work.

div.head: 1, MATTER' FOR DISCUSSION,
div.p: 1, MATTER' FOR DISCUSSION,

Th-e;;;ti-g-g-e—s tlon-s-1;;;1;;;offer—ed in the way of friendly criticism. It is very gratifying to find the leaders of the textile operatives committed to a forty eight hours week. The way to carry out that is a very proper matter for debate and enquiry. I have always urged that it is better to limit the day's work than the week's work, and I think I have the support of every economic authority on this question. The Bill is not likely to pass this year, but it is a good thing it has been introduced, because it will get the whole question discussed. It is one which is fully ripe for legislation. It is nearly forty years since there was any reduc- tion in the hours in cotton factories, except the 12 o'clock stop which only took off one hour a week.

I was pleased to see Mr. Stout's letter on this subject. I forget which of our English Bishops it was who once prefaced a pohlic utterance with the remark, " We are none of on infallible—not even the youngest" ; and I am myself too old to lay claim to anything like inerrancy. But methinks my kindly critic doth protest too much. Because I owned eceptisclem in relation to them "un-called sciences," and then went on to show how a shrewd old fortune- teller and student of human nature happened to make • lucky guess or a successful deduction from certain charscterietiminconsistency inlaid tome charge. With due deference I submit that the sentences which Mr. Stoat puts in contrast are complimentary, as they : were meant to he, and not contradictory or trreconctl- able. However, the head and front or my offending seems to be that I wrote lightly and even slightingly of phrenology. Is phrenolopy a science falsely to called ? That appears to be the question; and I have hi.herto supposed that in case of any competent judge of such matters only one answer was possible—the one I indicated. I willingly concede that physiognomy has its message, and I " from the top-sawyers ''uctfyersottothmatere"lll3urmofsobelse(rasn'd cheaper) exponents," pay great heed to that, and, indeed, rely merrily upon it, the bump-feeling or palm-scrutiny being merely so muck hocus-pocus, calculated to atoms the mystery- loving subject of his or her money's worth. TB E TWENTY-NINTH.

iliron-daYi•Si 'wee ' -Royal Oak Day. When I was • youngster, we never failed ti remind our school- master of its recurrence, quoting the old verse which, after setting forth the historic fact, ended thus significantly—" If you don't give us holiday we'll all ran away." The date is associated with the reetora. tins of the Monarchy in England. John Evelyn, himself an attached Royalist, witnessed the proceesion and, under date May 29th, his diary contains this record .—'This day His Majesty, Charles the Second, came to London, after a sad and long exile and calamitous suffering both cf the King and Church, being seventeen years. This was also Ma birthday, and with a triumph Ed above 20,000 horse and foot, brandishing their swords, and ehonting with inexpres- sible joy ; the ways strewed with flowers, the belle ringing, the streets hung with tapestry, fountains running with wine ; the Mayor, Aldermen, and all the Companiea, in their liveries, chains of gold. and banners, Lords and Nobles, clad in cloth of silver gold, and velvet ; the sindows nail balconies, all net with ladies ; trumpet., music, and myriads of people flocking, even so far as from Roc heater, so aa they were seven hours in passing the city, even f rein two in the afternoon till nine at night. I stood in the Strand and beheld it, and blessed God. And all this was done without one drop of blood abed, and by that very army which rebelled against him." It may be added that on the 25th January, 1685, less than a fortnight betore the King's death, the grieved Evelyn had to make this sad confession :—" Dr. Dore preached before the King. I saw this evening such a scene of profuse gaming, and the King in the midst of his three concubines, as I have never liefore seen-- luxurious dallying and profaneness." One prefer, ato draw the veil over the closing scenes of the reign which was inaugurated amid such great rejoiciags on the 29th May a quarter of a century before. MR. MITCHELL AND THE SCOUTS. In opposition to an overwhelming majority of the Warrington rluardians, I have taken my stand with the Rev. A. M. Mitchell when I thought that doughty member of the Board to be in the right. Shall I com- mend him for his action upon the Boy Scout move- ment ? I commend him not. If, like Mr. Stout, he had duly read, marked, learneiLand inwardly digeeted these weekly jottings, he would never have shown himself so ill-informed as to denounce the wonderful and most useful organisation in queetion as " a military movement." If there's one thing in mu- nection with it that all concerned, from the chief officer to the humblest and most obscure subordinate, have laboured to disaboae the public mind of, it is this idea that, notwithstanding all that those in authority have written and otherwise urged, Mr. Mitchell has somehow got into his head. Not long ago at Crewe, General Sir Robert Baden-Powell inepected over 1,101/ Cheshire Boy Scouts. Later he addreesel a public meeting with the idea of familiarising the public with the aim,, the Boy Scout movement. He emphasised the fact that it had nothing to do with soldiering. He was anxious that there should be a total absence of military discipline, which tended to discourage individual initiative. Ile prophesied an early development of the work on the lines of technical education and handi- crafts, and said the leaders were striving towards a closer relationship of the Scouts' organieation and evening continuation school.. I should very much like to add a summary of Scout law, but I must reserve this for the present. I am sure that, if Mr. Mitchell will lay aside his prejudice and look at the matter fairly, he will have to acknowledge that he han done the Boy Scouts and their leaders an injuatice. Tbat be did this in ignorance is clear,

The line in question bad been open but a little while when a woman who had travelled over it MOTO than once invited a neighbour to try the experiment. The latter was delighted with the journey, and reyeatedly expressed her pleasure CO as to be heard throughout the comportment. Then an accident occurred, and the pony were thrown down a abort embankment, trickily they were none the worse for the startling experience, and their good humour was fully restored when the one who was travelling by I train for the first time innocently exclaimed, " Well, it's been a grand ride, bat they've rather. rough way landin"em at th' fur end! In his Sankey Bridges Wesleyan anniversary lectbre the Rev. John Ken3ick mentioned that Bunyan was once brought before the magiterateo for not attending church. The other day • friend of mine who collects such things showed me copy of a summons for the like offence issued by Lancashire Justices in 1810 --within living memory that is, the churchwarden s had taken the name of a labourer whom they found loitering in the vicinity of the churh during divine service. The man drcliaed to attend church, and was reported, convicted, awl fined a shilling and coots. Lacking the wherewithal to pay, he was committed to prison in default. A note in another column a week ago suggests an allusion to the beginning of our popular autnmer re,time. An acraintance of mine who writes on mincellaneoue topicn pointe out that the name itself in derived from cric (Saxon), a crooked slick. A bat and bell game was plaped in the 13th century. Hy authority proceeds : 'Ad Indendos ad creag " (Edw. 1.) ; first use of word approaching the modern term. 1315, fielders first introduced. In the 15th century knows as " Hondyn" or " Hondoute" (Hand in or hand out). Interdicted as illegal by statute (171 Edw. IV.), because it wan thought lobe detri- mantel to the practice of archery. The word Crickett was first used about 1570. In 1748 (Anne) its illegality wan purged, and Cricket wan pronounced by a judical decision to be • "very manly game." The first Cricket Club was founded in 1750, and was called the Hambledon Club. It fell into decay and came to an end towards the end of the century. The wao founded in 17A7. div.head: DROWNED WHILE GATHERING FLOWERS. –
div.p: DROWNED WHILE GATHERING FLOWERS. -
The Inquest.

Mr. Y. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inonest at the Polio, Station on Diureday on the body of Evelyn Derbyehire, the nine-year old daughter of William Derbyshire 4, Sutton-street, who was drowned in the river near the weir at How ley on Monday evening. Elizabeth Derbyshire, mother of tbe deeeesed, raid ' she lest new bee daughter alive at 7.15 on Monday evening, when she brought her some buttercup.. Hal f- an-hour later she heard that deceased had been drowned. Her daughter bad often gorse to the riser- Bide with other children to pick buttercups. Wanesu had always replied' No " when the child had caked if she could Co. Evelyn ilulam, aged 7, end lining at 8, Sutton-greet, said the deceased celled for her on Monday evening and asked if she would go end pick some buttercups by the river. While so doing the deceased fell in and dragged the witness with her.

' 7Villi;OTO-we; ifiWards, said that while walking along the river aide on Monday, he saw two men trying to get the girl lisslam out of the water. When she was rescued she told them about the other girl being in the water. lie went and got some gremlins irons and efter throwing them in shout three times he recovered the body. Artificial respiration wee resorted to for about half en hour, baton the arrival of two doctors, life was pronounced to be extinct. The body had only been In the water from seven to ten minutes.

Albert how e, a moulder, said while going home along the river bank he heard • cry for help. Ile went to the river aide, and there saw the girl Haalam in the water. Ile jumped in and succeeded in rescuing her. The jury returned • verdict of " Accidental death," and it was decided to make • animation to the police to draw the attention of the TO4III Council to the advis- ability of having a countable on duty in the vicinity of the Weir during the children's summer holidays. Albeit Lowe WU also commended for his his bravery in rescuing the other girl.

div.head: PEACE AND WAR.
div.p: PEACE AND WAR.
"THE GREAT ILLUSION."
Does the Victorious Nation Benefit?
By C. E. Parker.

Mr. Norman Angell has written a book entitled "The Great Illusion" in which he advances arguments to prove from an economic standpoint that war is, not alone destructive to the economical and'commercial advancement of the conquered nation, but that, under modern conditions, the victorious nation suffers out of all proportion to any material advantage gained by conquest. He; sets out to prove that military and political' power gives a nation no commercial advan- tage, that it is an economic impossibility for one nation to seize or destroy what creates the wealth of another, or for one nation to enrich itself by subjugating another. The author challenges the almost universally accepted idea that the wealth and prosperity of defenceless nations are at the mercy of ' stronger ones. The argument may not be altogether a new one, and in parts may be carried too far, but I doubt if it has ever been put forward with such conciseness and force as in "The Great Illusion."

The book has created a great deal of interest, not alone in this country but in many parts of Europe. It has been freely criticised, but very few of the critics have attacked or tried to answer the main contentions of the work. Most of the reviewers have taken the line adopted by Sir Edward Grey in his speech at the Argentine Centenary Banquet at which he said : When I read that Leek I was reminded o' the isa3hig of • thinker • great ninny years ago that it is not things that matter an much, but people'. opinions abmt things. True au the shaman( of that book maybe, it does not become an operative movement in the minds and conduct of nations until they are convinced of its truth, and it has become a commonplace to them." Mr. Angell is in entire agreement with Sir Edward Grey. He recognises that general disarmament is at present out of the ques- tion. His book is not written to advocate this. It is written to " change people's opinions about things," to get the nations of the world to overhaul their conceptions as to the utility of war, to bring the thinking unite which compose the nations face to face with the truth as the author sees it. His book is a challenge to all who believe in war as a necessary, or profitable, part of a nation's development. If the "statement of that book be true" then may we not expect that "people's opinions" will change in the direction of the truth as stated? If the main contentions in the "Great Illusion " can be made good, and become a matter of common knowledge, it would give a tremendous impulse to the movement towards peace. This movement for the present derives its propelling power, not so much from economic and material considerations (indeed it is frequently upon such grounds that the plea for big armaments is based) as from those which belong to the ethical, moral, and religious spheres. Our author in the main puts these aside, his feet are ever on the ground, and his arguments appeal to those whose interests are in the main limited to material considerations. It will at once be realized that if those whose vision is bounded by material interests, who never ascend to the higher reaches, if it could be proved to such that both for themselves,and for the nation of which they form units,war must always result in material loss, both to victor and vanquished, what a powerful addition there would be to those who oppose war. If such united their interest to those of the humanitarian, the idealist, and the Christian, the era of univereal peace among nations would be clearly in sight. THE ARGUMENT.

To grasp the full force °Abe argument of the book it is necessary carefully to read it, but I hope to be able within the limits of two or three papers in your journal to give some idea of the main lines of argument. Our author lays great emphasis on the changed conditions of modern civilisation as com- pared with those of the past ; he emphasizes this again and again. He admits that in the past it was possible for the conqueror to profit by conquest, as for instance when tribute could be exacted, or when the strongest and most useful sections of the conquered people could be transported to the conquering country, and made to work for the conqueror, as of old. He contends that our thoughts on war are dominated by terms and ideas which were only applicable to conditions which the development of our civilisation has altogether abolished. He speaks of " the illusion" due to the hypnotism of an obsolete terminology. And, considered in the light of modern con- ditions, he goes on to affirm that "No nation can in our day by military conquest perma- nantly,or for any considerable period,destroy, or greatly damage, the trade of another,aince trade depends upon the existence of natural wealth, and a population capable of working it. So long as the natural wealth of the country and the population to work it remain, an invader cannot 'utterly destroy it' as affirms a modern writer. He could only destroy the trade by destroying the population, which is not practicable, and if he could destroy the population he would destroy his own market, actual or potential, which would he commercially suicidal." Here then we see one of the main lines of argument. The material interests of nations are now so aglutinated that what damages one reflects upon all others, and especially on the conqueror. Suppose for example it came to pass, as suggested in the question of a fiery patriot in a London newspaper: "If the German army invaded England and looted the cellars of the Bank of England, and carried off the founda- tions of our whole national fortune, what then would happen?" What rubbish to speak of sovereigns as the foundations of our whole national fortune. Germany's financial stability depends nearly as much upon our bank reserve as does our English finance. The first effect of such action would be a run on every bank in England. But simultane- ously German hankers, many with credits in London, would feel the effect, merchants the whole world over threatened by ruin through the collapse in London would immediately call in all their credits in Germany, and German finance would present l a condition of things hardly less chaotic than that in England. It is as certain as anything can be,that were the German army guilty of such economic vandalism, there is no considerable institution in Germany that would escape grave damage—damage in credit and security, so serious as to constitute , a lose immensely greater than the value of the loot obtained. But very much the same I effect would result from a declaration of war between the two countries and this without any act of burglary of the bank reserve stored in the cellars of the Bank of England. Germany's capital and credit, because of the I internationalisation and political interdepend- ence of our modern financial system would also suffer severely. Not only would the

individuals trading with England suffer, but the whole commercial community would laic,. A French authority puts the question of the increasing interdependence of nations in regard to financial matters in the following words : The rapid development of industry hes given rim, to the active intervention of finance,which has become the nerrits rertirs, soil hair come to play a dominating role under the influence of finance; industry is beginning to lose its exclusively national character, to tate on a character more and more international. The animosity of rival nationalities seems to be in a process of attenua- tion is a result of this increasing international solidarity." lam not sure if this is quite the correct way of putting the situation. It in possible that rival national animosities are not under- going very rapid attenuation, but this is certain, that more and more as industry and finance become international, and every year grow in magnitude and influence, those important sections of every nation whose financial and industrial interests will be jeopardized by war, will, for their own material safety, restrain those in power from plunging their country into war. ANNEXED TERRITORY.

_ .... The seizing of territory which belor.gs to the vanquished is one form of advantage by which a victorious nation is supposed to gain. But what advantage is such forcible appro- priation to the conqueror? In every modern civilized state, revenues drawn from a territory acquired are expended on that territory, and tribute is not levied for use of the central state. The seizing of Alsace- Lorraine by Germany in the Franco-German war instead of increasing Germany's wealth has impoverished it. By the acquisition German has now a more extended frontier to protect, considerable sums have been drawn from the German tax-payer to build defences on the new boundary, and a vast army has to be supported to safeguard the new territory. What German is a halfpenny the better for the acquisition of Alsace-Lorraine? What material advant- age has Germany gained ? The inhabitants of these new dominions would be of doubtful value to Germany should the soreneses left in France by the seizure of this territory flame out in war. INDEMNITIES. It may be contended that the indemnity which France paid to Germany should be taken at its face value as an advantage which could be set in part against the enormous cost of this war, and be taken as an illustration how the conqueror can gain by war. But even an indemnity is of doubtful value, and is subject to an enormous dis- count. It would be ridiculous to overstate the argument by contending that the conquered nation gained by the paying of an indemity and that the conqueror loses. At the same time the financial and economic conditions of France and Germany during. and for some time after, the payment of the indemnity suggest some interesting features bearing upon the question. Mr. Angell points out that the decade from 1870 to 1880 was for France a great recuperative period, and for Germany, after a" boom" in 1872 one of depression. No less an authority than Bismarck himself testifies to the double fact. We know that Bismarck's life was clouded by watching what appeared to him an absurd miracle ; the regeneration of France after the war taking place more rapidly and more completely than the regeneration in Ger- many, to such an extent that in introducing his Protectionist Bill in 1879 he declared "that Germany was slowly bleeding to death, and that if the present process was continued she would find herself ruined." . . _

M. Block in 1879 said "If we only could get back to the general position of things before the war, but salaries diminish and prices go up." He adds "The five milliards provoked a rapid increase in import giving rise to extravagance, and as soon as the effect of the expenditure of the money had passed there was a slackening." Between the years 1872 and 1877 the deposits in the State Savings Bank in Germany actually fell by roughly 20 per cent, while in the same period the French deposits increased by about 20 per cent. The looting of the cellars of the Bank of England and the payment to an indemnity stand much on the same footing as far as their effects on the conquering country are concerned Suppose Germany got possession of a large amount of French or English gold by an indemnity or by plundering the Bank of England, what could it do with it? Surely the veriest novice must know that the only thing that can enrich a country is goods, not currency. During the siege of Paris there were millions in the cellars of the Banks of France. Suppose these had been distributed— they would not have fed a single child. The money would only have been useful if it could have been taken outside the b sieged city to purchase food. In the same way for Germany or any other country to get a supply of gold in excess of its own wants for purpose of exchange would be useless. Indemnities must be paid for in goods. Now normal imports called for by the wants of the community are healthy and enriching, but abnormal spasmodic imports created by depreciation of the currency due to an excess of coin are of very questionable advantage. But grant if we will that an indemnity is a material gain, it shrinks into nothingness when we reckon the direct cost of war, the preparations for it, and the far greater indirect loss by the dislocation of national finance and its effect on industry. The influence of the payment of an indemnity in the event of a victory by Germany over England would mean to Germany the impoverishment of her best customer. We should send goods to Germany in payment of the indemnity instead of sending goods to pay for those we at present buy from Germany. The balance of trade based on , exchange would be upset and individual firms in both countries crippled. Germany at present largely relies on the financial stability of this country. If this were under- mined as the result of war all German enterprises, the credit of which is buttressed by British finance, would be endangered.
(To be contt.usel.)

div.head: WARRING TON MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
div.p: WARRING TON MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
NOTABLE CHORAL COMPETITIONS.

For some years Warrington lion played a worthy part in that commendable competitive movement which a having such a stimulating and refining influerce upon fits musical life of our time. Not only have local choirs won their laurels in some of the leading contests in the North, bo t the Warrington Musical Festival has acquired a reputation for the high standard of talent which it annually attracts from a wide area. Too much praise cannot be accorded to that enthusiastic hand of pioneers, the Warringtm Apollo Choir, who, in face of apathy and discouragement, founded the festival and achieved for it a recognized place in Lancashire competitive circles. Four years ago the enterprise aas Oared up, n a broader and more representative hrois mid its usefulness consider- ably extended. It cannot, however, be said that the -support of the music-1 .ving public of War. ington has been commensurate with the magnitude cf the under- taking, but, in spite of stinted reeourcenthe committee ban never allowed its optimism to be shaken. The C‘tronati.m Festival, which was held in the Parr Hall on Saturday, was particularly gratifying from the tnusical point of view, but the comparative meagrencas of the local patrnmtge was °gain ale
MR. NATHAN 000 K.

appointieg. Of course, the out-door charm, of an ideal May day must have kept many people away, but the committee c add not be blamed for h, lding the event Co late in the year, as the fact that no many of the leading festivals are being held at this time was a great help in securing entries, which excelled all previous record., the competitors nuobering over 1,100. II in for the excellence of its choral competi- tions that the Guonation festival will chiefly be remembered. The principal choral contest for mixed choirs attracted nine of the best known organisations of Lancashire, and their singing provided a rich treat. The selected pieces " Who is Sylvia" (7ermant and " Let their celestial concerts all unite " (Uantle/) onstituted a fairly severe test of the capabilities of the choiss, the stirring Handel chorus being particularly exacting. It was evident to a'l who followed the con- test close'y that the hem tura lay Venoms Southport Choir and Sale and Di -trict Mueical Society, each cf which pnes.ses a magnificent body of voices under splendid control The Southport choir triumphed by a single point and thus become holders far twelvo months of the beaatiful shield presented by Mrs. A.ll. Crosfield,as well as rt ceiving a earth prize of The male voice choir competition was also one of the finest ever beard in Lancashire, interest in it being increased by the fact that the seven entrants included the two local choirs. "The long day closes" Sullican) and " 'l'o Celia "(C. Lee William.), were two delight fui and well contrasted test tines and they received painstaking and effective treatment from moist of the competitors. The victory of the Gorton Male Voice MK, was well deserved and the Warrington Male Voice Choir was a pool second. The children's choir competition gave rise to healthy local rivalry and it was indeed pleatdng to Sad conductors who are wiling to devote their time to training the young in the vocal art. The Warrington Secondary School choir sang' 0 ! The flowery month of June " (Jackson) in a really charmiEg manner and unquestionably stood oat as superidl. to the other six choirs. The second sward went to Brick-street Sunday School choir a very promising and enthusiastic body of young singers. One of the most pleasing features of the festival was
Sprnce, W Ivnodeock, J W Willett, E Wilk.; treasurer, Mr Thome. Brouglt ; anietxnt Ferrel ary, Mr Flank Rickman ; general Eecretaly, Mr R W Cook.
REGRETS FOR NON-ATTENDANCE.

Mr. Harold Smith had written., follows :—" Benne of Commons Library, May 24. My dear sir—lt is with very coal regret that I find that it is quite impossible for me to attend your musical festival on Saturday next. I think I told you that I would make a great effort to attend and would certainly do no unless some unforeseen chorea rendered it impossible. I now find that I have an important engagement on Saturday in London, and I could not powiibly get to Warrington in time. I know that I shall miss a great musical treat, which will be largely attended by an appreciative audience.—Youry siccerely, lJsnoti, Semi. It. W. Cook, Esq " Letters and telegrams of apology for inability to attend were ale received from Sir Gilbert' Oreenall, , Bart., Mr. and Mrs. A. 11. Croefield and Mrs. Garnett, of Penketh.

Speaking of the Gorton Male Voice Choir, to .hom the , prize was awarded, Dr. McNaught said this choir ' arrested his attention the moment it beg or, Its singing , of " The long day closes '' wan SO smooth, clean and ' well-finished. There was a rhythmic charm about it , all ; they realized the moods, and the purity of it was ' splendid. In short it was a very fine performance. In , "To Celia" they beam vela. fervenr ; then the ' pianissimo was capital, the mock deqgair excellent. He thought the speciality of this Choir noun unity of , colour. At the end they got a regular belfry of sound. With regard to the Warrington Male Voice Choir ' their singing of "The long day closes " was, to hie tame, a lit! le slow, end be would rather have • little more movement. They were well controlled and moody. The tostoluto stun good. Ile could not help listening to them and being charmed. The subdued tone' were very effective indeed. The tone aes a very line blend, hut at "faith dispose." it was not revealed , very properly. There were no juleps; It was beautiful. The Brut tenors or altos fell off a little in intonntlon. A magnificent tine round climes was secured. The pinnimiroo was always very delicate. In "To Celia" there was impetuosity and they gem the right emphasis. The vowels were well defined and the not. I burst/ were dramatic. The piece was brought out

apiendidly. The feature of the performance waa the vehement intensity of the expression. The 'Warrington Apollo choir'. rendering of "The long day closes," showel good realization of the mood at the start, hot on, perhaps louder than it ought to 'lave hetn. Very smooth, well polished, much warmth and paasiosx—a well equipped choir. There were 000 00 two beautiful notes. 'To Celia" was fluent, and caught the mood of dermalr. Music improved the spirit and elevated the tone of the mind and it had even a beneficial effect upon the body. Referring to great musieans of the past the Mayor expressed the opinion that English composers like Ptercell were worthy to rank with Mozart, Haydn and other foreign muter., but English names did not sound so great. (Laughter). The musicians of the past struggled often against poverty aud bad a difficulty in holding their own. They were like the bees who had made tbe honey for on to eat sod we ought to feel grateful to them for their efforts. They very rarely made fortunes—in fact he believed the rieturre of the present day would often make no much laser evening as carol thmo great oomposers made in a year. In spite of all those precautions, however, Handel found means of gratifying his ambition. The men who patonised the poor composers of the past were mainly royalty and the aristocracy. IRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
AN ISSUE OF IMPERIAL IMPORT.

Perhaps the moat no!eworthy of the speeches by which leading Irishmen have endeavoured to enlighten English public 0011100 in Great Britain on the Irish Natknal Demand was that which was delivered by Mr. John Redmond a few darn ago in Essex. It folownd a strikingly courageous nod eloquent address from Sir John Simon. If all his colleagues in the Liberal tarty be of the mind of the Solicitor. General for England—and he declared he spoke for them as well as liiinrelf—justice will surely be done to Ireland. Sir John p'eaded that it should be (lore at once. The s nisions of the Imperial Confer- ence furnished him with a text, which he need with Sect. England, at peace with her aelf-g 'yarned Colonies, can reckon upon their deep and abiding I .valty, beeatme they are free. The rights of races which made war agaiust her have been recognised and cone,xled. Thedeeds of men standing for such recognition, Dutchmen and French Canadian alike, hare been forgotten- in the case of Ireland the wound ban been kept open. It WIN dis- tinctly ocouraging to an Iri.dman to find an English meeting accepting .d applauhng no heartily Sir John Simon's tribute to the democratic spirit of Ireland's Nationalist representatives, who, although burdened by the cares of • land so long and so con- sistently mingoverned, have ever been " foremost champions in every measure for the improvement of the conditions of the masses in Great Britain." Mr. Redmond quite properly pointed neat that the refoln lesired was reared by Irish votes. In no instance were the democracies more completely in true accord then in the long struggle to be terminated by the placing of the Veto Bill on the Statute Book. The power of the Lords that oppress the people is dead -dead an a door nail in the language of Dickens—and with the ditappearance of the rule of privilege and class, a new era of hope is opened for Great Britdn an well as far Del md. Home Rule is only one, though the greatest at the moment of the measures of justi. upon which the peers cannot in future wreak their will. Mr. Redmond's confidence and Sir John Simon's earnettness will inspire confi- dence in the minds of the 16nh at borne and what in of almost equal importance in the minds of Liberals in Great Britain. As on former occasiona, the Leader of the Irish rople t sachet upon all the phases ,of the q tied ion spar which Englishmen desired information. Re defined Ireland's

demand as a demand fr tlpt lone Rule which Parnell desired, and that Parnell did not contemplale sepsis- lion his statements rn oath before the Parnell Corn- minion most emphatically prove. Mr. Redmond ,hewed that John Bull in the interests of Ilia pocket would be wise to concede the Irish demand at once. Truly enough, English flounce experts have shear. that 1 ha Pull has obtained from Ireland during the Mat ninety-three years 325 millet. over and above the cost of governing that country, but the two million surplus which Mr. Gledsmne's stltesruanlike mind apprehended

no it'd be swallowed on by the government f Ireland has already vanished —alms rendering only too real one of that great Englishman's prophecies shoot the question lie !alt.-sired no heroically to solve. Mr. Redmond was therefore abundantly justified in saying to the Englishmen of Walthamstow" the longer Home Rule is postponed the greater will be your loss." Apart from the financial obligation, based as it is on the findings of an D.glish Royal Commiesion, there in always to be borne In mind that quickening cause of decay which was the legislation, a; infamous., any Penal Law, lif•ignei and passed for the ratio, lion of Irish induteries. Mr. Balfour himself has designated this as a cruel and stupid process which demanded restitution, and an oppleunity for being just, if not generous, will satin arms. In the fine words of Sr John Simon it will be an opportunity for all lovers of Britain's Empire to right a wrong "in the place where it presses most distressiogly on our memories end upon our responsibilities." THE CENSUS IN IRELAND.

The preliminaty report of the Irish Census Com- mis.ioners eontait 03 surprise for the observer of social conditions in Ireland. No student of these matter of fact but at the same time heart-breaking reports issued by the Registrar-General could have expected that the statistics of Malt population would shim an increase. Later on we will take the oppor- laxity to examine a little more closely these vitally important Irish figures For the moment it is euffi- dent to note that between 1901 and 1911 a decrease of 76,824 hoe occurred in the population of Ireland. while the figure. for England, Scotland and Wales record an all-round increase. To put the facts in another form, it is a melancholy thought for any refloctive mind to note that of all the wide and scattered dominions of the Empire, Ireland alone sheers Euch • disastrous decline.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SA rURDAY. JUNE 3 19IL
Those members of the MR. CHURCHILL House of Commons AND HIS who did not go down to CRITICS. Epsom on Wednesday

had an exciting time of their own at Westminster. Mr. CHURCHILL was being baited by gentlemen opposite just in the style that was common when Mr. GLADSTONE was at the head of the 1880 Government and the Home Secretary's father was the leader of the Fourth Party. It is our own opinion that, apart from the tumult by which he was silenced, Mr. CHURCHILL did not get fair play. In -the first place, Mr. Eamon', who is acting as Deputy-Speaker during Mr. LowTHER's absence, does not appear -to have been exactly informed as to the expressions used by the HOME SECRETARY on Tuesday night. What Mr. CHURCHILL said was not really an expression of his own opinion. He was describing what he believes to be a rather general impression among the working dames of the country as a consequence of such occurrences as the Taff Vale decision and the Osborne judgment, " It is unfortunate," he observed, " that an impression prevails among the working classes that the Courts are biassed (uncon- sciously, no doubt) in cases affecting indus- trial interests." We fail to see what any reasonable person can object to in the words just quoted. The HOME SECRE- TARY did not speak of the Judges,l but of the courts. He was not expressing views of his own, but reporting some of those which find expression elsewhere. And finally, he went out of his way to suggest that if the courts are biassed in certain cases the bias is no doubt unconscious. It suited

gentlemen on the Conservative benches to assume that Mr. CHURCHILL was making an attack on the Judges, and to make so much noise that it was difficult to hear what he said, and almost impossible to follow his actual meaning. These, at any rate, are the facts, as we now understand them. Mr. LvTrELTON's argument was that even giving full weight to the word " unconsciously" there was a direct imputation of incompetence on the part of the greatest Judges in this country. There was, as we have shown, nothing of the kind, and it was certainly not Mr. CHURCHILL who ought to have been called upon to withdraw. There is an old adage which affirms that one man may steal a horse though another may not so much as look over the hedge. The HOME SECRETARY is the man to whom look- ing over the hedge is forbidden. His mere appearance at the table of the House of Commons usually makes his opponents furiously angry. What he says does not so much matter. It is the fashion to interrupt, misinterpret, and insult him. Mr. LYTTELTON lies back and smiles when he is accused of a monstrous misrepresentation. The smile does not appear to have much appropriateness to the circumstances. man accused of a monstrous mis- representation should have some other sort of reply at•his command. Probably Mr. CHURCHILL knows as well as Mr. Emmorr or Mr Lvrrguog that Judges ought not to be attacked except on a specific motion. The point is that he did not attack the Judges; and there can be little doubt, we believe, that at least those members of the working classes who are members of Trade Unions really are under the impression that their unions do not get fair play in the courts. There may be no foundation what- ever for this view of the facts. But to say that such a view exists is not to endorse it, and to rule that a member of Parliament ought not to speak in the House about 1 opinions which he finds to be prevalent out, of doors when they have a bearing on the conduct of high servants of the Crown whose impartiality is a tradition would be to limit very considerably and quite unnecessarily the area of party discussion.
A not very pretty THE CHILDREN AND squabble has arisen CORONATION DAY, over the prop osal of

the Coronation Com- mittee to celebrate the occasion on June 22nd by a great children's demonstration in Victoria Park. The Committee seem to have fixed upon this plan and then called in the teachers to carry out details. At this point difficulties arose, for the teachers found objections more or less insuperable to con- veying 14,000 children—some as young as 4 years—to a remote " centre " like Victoria Park by way of the congested Warrington Bridge and Knutsford-road, and then feeding, managing, and re-collecting them. They offered an alternative suggestion, but , the Committee appears to have taken I umbrage and abandoned the whole scheme, while throwing the blame upon the teachers. At Monday's meeting of the Education Committee some rather injudicious remarks were made about the " selfishness" of the teachers, which have embittered rather than bettered the situation. The teachers can well defend themselves against the charge seeing that they were pledged to give the day to the children if desired. What we are concerned with, Is the consideration of causes which go further back. Weeks ago Iwe expressed doubt of the wisdom of holding Walking Day on the day following the Coro- nation. How were the children to find time, strength and enthusiasm for two such celebrations in forty-eight hours. Father Wilson voiced the same criticism, and if more serious attention had been paid to it the present impasse and public exasperation might have been avoided. Apparently the children are to be left to" coronate "in their own sweet way, and carry out the usual Walking Day festival on the following day. Frankly, we hardly see how they could have been expected to do more, and if the Corona- tion falls flat from the children's point of view the blame must rest on those who decided to have Walking Day in the same week.

The Mothers' and THE MOTHERS' B a hies' Welcome, AND BABIES' which is to be inaugu- WELCOME, rated next Wednesday at the Academy-street schools, should prove an interesting social experiment, especially with the possibility of a hot summer with its special dangers to infant life. This is the practical outcome of the educational campaign regarding infantile mortalityicarried on in our columns and else- where. Public opinion was deeply stirred, I and it became evident that any forward movement made by the Health Committee would receive enthusiastic support. After several months of careful consideration a happy working alliance seems to have been set up between the Health Committee and the Guild of Help. The Guild has been wise enough to hand over the practical working of the scheme to a representative committee of ladies with Miss Margaret Broadbent as honorary secretary. Many towns have already similar centres, which are long past the experimental stage, and have proved wonderfully useful to working I mothers and their infants. No doubt the I scheme in Warrington will avoid elabora- tion, but extensive developments may follow if the present simple clan should prove successful.
The Lords have passed
A STRATEGICAL the BeCOnel Reading of MOVEMENT TO THE the Parliament Bill REAR. without a division.

Lord Morley reminded the Lords who made this unwilling conces- sion to the cumulative force of democratic sentiment, that such a formal concession would have no value if it was followed up by an attempt to mutilate the government measure in committee. Of course the passing of the Second Reading may be only a move in the Tory game of tactics. But that game has never led to anything but humiliation. However that may be, the Lords have admitted that the feeling of the nation is against them, and has been against them, in a kind of crescendo scale, ever since the Budget of 1909 was rejected.
The provisions of the THE TRADE Trade Unions Bill. UNIONS BILL which revises the

position of Trade Unions under the Osborne decision, are simple. If a majority, obtained by ballot, so decides, a Trade Union may take part in political work, as before the decision, but any trade unionist may by written notice "contract out" of
contributing to the political fund. In spite of a heated scene the Bill passed its Second Reading by a majority of 201. Lord
Rosebery bat!
A VERY "CROSS- never made so typical BENCH " ArrrrunE. a "cross-bench "speech

as that with whiCh he signalised the rout and discomfiture of Tory- ism before the triumphant progress of the Bill which lays it down, as a fundamental principle ot the British Constitution, that the will of the people shall be the final arbiter of the " destinies of Empire," over which Mr. Balfour formerly assured the Tories I that they enjoyed a prescriptive right. Lord Rosebery all but taunted the Opposition with 1 cowardice for not rejecting the Bill. Yet he I assured them that the result of two General Elections could not be ignored, and that they were incapable of carrying on the business of the country if they insisted on rejecting the I Bill, and a new Government was conse- lquently needed.

The Corporation Bill has at last received the Royal assent and it is expected that a st trt will be made with the new bridge works next week. • • •
Germany has ex;resred her willingness to enter into negotiations with the United States for general arbitration on the lines of IPresident Taft's draft treaty.

Mrs. Churchill, the wife of the Home Secretary, gave birth to a son on Monday morning, at 33, Eccleston Square, Mr. Churchill's London House. Mr. and Mrs. Churchill's other child is a daughter. *4* _ .

Special Coronation issues of the "Examiner 'S will be published on Saturday, June 17th, and Saturday, June 24th. Each issue will contain an illustrated art-paper inset, printed in Royal purple—a feature which proved so immensely popular with our readers on the occasion of King Edward's visa in 1909. • •

One of the dangers of taking 14,000 children to Victoria Park for Coronation day ' has been emphasised in a tragic manner this ' week. Two little children were picking buttercups on the river bank on Monday when both fell into the water and one was frowned. The river-side is just as much inprotected where it bounds the Park and there would have been great anxiety and responsibility for those in charge if the scheme to entertain the children in the Park had gone forward.

rhe days of the Roman occupation of Wilderspool have been commemorated by a tablet provided by the industrious Warring- ton Society, and affixed high upon the Brewery wall. An onlooker at the unveiling ceremony on Tuesday remarked somewhat unkindly that to place such a tablet on the wall of a brewery was the saddest evidence of the decline of Rome that he had seen. The tablet is firmly fixed, and unless Mr. Lloyd- George fulfils the worst predictions of his foes by taxing breweries out of existence, it should bear testimony for long years to come that the noble Roman—the pioneer of civilization—once encamped on the land adjoining.

A musical treat but disappointing attend- ances were again characteristics of the Warrington Musical Festival on Saturday,. It is strange that Ararrington, which has some claim to be regarded as a musical centre, does not show a more practical interest in this effort of a few of the more enthusi- astic townsmen to promote and encourage musical culture in our midst. Judged by the entries the festival excelled all previous enterprises of the kind, and the various choral competitions will long be remembered with pleasure by all who heard them. Incidentally the different methods of conduct- ing formed a highly instructive study in themselves, and the audience almost held its breath when some of the more daring gentle- ' men came perilously near to falling off the chair on which they chose to perch them- selves in order to have a better command over their forces.

Mr. and Mrs. Croefierd yesterday had the pleasure of entertaining to lunch at 39, Hyde Park Gate, Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay MacDonald, Mr. D. J. Shackleton, Mr. Arthur Henderson, and Miss Sanger, Hon. Secretary of the British Section of the International Associa- tion for Labour Legislation. The party assembled to meet Mr. Schlytter to consider various ways and means by which it is hoped to the further the international movement for the abolition of twelve hours shifts in continuous processes, and the substitution of three shifts of eight hours each instead. Mr. Schlytter has taken the lead in this international movement, and the Association has appointed a Committee to make investigations in different countries and help the whole movement forward. Sir Thomas Oliver and Mr. Crosfield are the members of the British Section of this Com- mittee.

• • 1 We are glad to note (says the " West- minster Gazette ") that electricity is exonerated from all blame due for the Hulton colliery disaster, which would appear to have been due to a defective lamp. The more we can get electricity to light and work the mines the better and safer will life be to the man underground. There has been too much tendency to attribute fire and other disasters to electricity—which is ordinarily the safest of the forms of power with which we deal. Mr. Redmayne attempts to turn the tables by recommending the use of electric lamps in fiery mines. The present difficulty is that the really efficient lamp for the miner does not appear. Most varieties are heavy, cumbrous, and inefficient. The other day an offer of £l,OOO for a suitable lamp was made, and this may stimulate the electricians to as great a triumph as was achieved by Davy in an earlier day._

• • School hygiene is so nearly related to public health that the Education Committee I did a praiseworthy thing in holding a special ' meeting to consider their medical officer's annual report. Dr. Hibbert has criticised the schools as he has found them, and in many there are long-standing defects of sanitation and ventilation which seem beyond the powers of the best-intentioned school managers to remedy. "New schools for old ones" is apparently the only solution and while the ratepayer will doubtless endorse a progressive policy he merits rather more consideration than Alderman Bennett appears willing to give him when he says complacently that" the cry of the over- burdened ratepayer is overdone." The best feature of the meeting was the keen interest which every member manifested in the general question of improving the conditions by which the young life of the town will emerge from the chrysalis stage equipped with the knowledge and physique requisite for the battle of life.

Tuesday must have been a proud day for Mr. Thomas May, who for many years has devoted himself, in the face of scepticism and discouragement, to the exploration of the Roman Camp at Wilderspool. Warrington now recognizes the value of his work which, ta use Alderman Bennett's words, has definitely established the fame of the town as a Roman centre, and the Warrington Society was acting in accordance with its best traditions in marking this most historic spot in the locality by the provision of a commemoratory tablet on the adjoining building. It was high testimony indeed 1 which that eminent authority, Profr. W. Boyd rawkins, bore to the significance of the discoveries. They prove beyond all doubt that even in the days of the Romans IWarrington was a town of many industries. Iron, bronze, enamelling and glass work were amongst the occupations in which the Romans excelled and it is curious that in its subsequent history Warrington has so signally fulfilled the promise of those distant days. Verily there is nothing new under the sun

Entering at the Tower Lodge a walk of two miles past the lake revealed the charming natural beauties of Lord Delamere's estate at its very bent. Banks of rhododendrons are not a photographer's subject, bat they formed a delightful , theme for the eye of those who were merely visitors and there are few places out of the New Forest where these magnificent purple banks are more finely displayed. At the Pl. ugh Ina, Foxwist Green, tea was eagerly I enjoyed (I thick "eagerly "is the right adverb there) homely though the manner was ot serving it ; and several succensful pictures are the outcome of plate exposures on the pretty little jublic house. COACHING CLUBS' OPENING MEET IN THE PARK. The Coaching Club held its opening meet of the season in Hyde Park on Saturday, and drew an unusually large gatheting. The revival in Coaching was plain to all beholders, as the meet was larger than it has been for many seasons past. There were in all nineteen coaches lined up, as compared with twelve last year, and the parade was a sight that must have gladdened the eyes of all who have at heart the good of one of the most typical English pastimes, and one of the richest in all tradition. After the usual tour round the Park, the coaches started off for Hurlingham for luncheon. _ THE TWO MOST BRILLIANT PLANETS It is not often that we have the oppor- tunity of seeing our two most brilliant planets to such advantage as at the present time. As soon as the sun has set Venus shines out lovely and beautiful in the west and a few minutes later Jupiter may be seen in the south-west. We call Venus the evening star (though it is not a star at all) because it usually shines out first after the sun has gone down. Jupiter is not often seen to such advantage as Venus ; its orbit is long and it is at an immense distance from us. Compared with the Earth or with Mars or Venus, Jupiter would be as a football placed beside a marble. Seen through a telescope Jupiter is interest- ing for it is crossed by dusky bands and has an array of bright and dark markings. Venus although so beautiful has no interest when seen through the glass. Indeed we know very little about Venus and little can be discovered. This may come as a surprise especially when we remember that Venus is such a near neighbour to the earth. I want to advise all my readers to begin to take an interest in astronomy. If you know the names of the stars and planets the sky will always present a grand panoroma, and be much more interesting than any picture palace. By looking often at the planets their appearance will become familiar and we are able to recognize them whenever they appear, and now is a very good time to make the acquaintance of Venus and Jupiter. " Gracious, Tommy," said the startled visitor, "I never saw a lad get as many spankings as you dot Why, it seems to be a continuous performance down in the wood- shed l" " Oh, I can stand it," laughed Tommy, with a wink. " You can 'stand it?" queried the !visitor. "Easily. When dad spanks me, ma feels so sorry ishe gives me sweets on the sly; and when ma spanks me, dad feels so sorry he gives me twopence and takes me to see the cricket match.' THE BIGGINT BUTTERFLY. Boys are interested in butterflies, though not always kind to them, and it occurs to me total! them about the biggest butterfly that has yet been found. It has been discovered only in British New Guinea and specimeui are so scarce that they are bought by collectors at £2O each. The male measures eight inches across the wings and the female not less than eleven inches, a wing spread exceeding that of many small birds. The story of the first discovery of this gigantic butterfly is a curious one. A naturalist saw a specimen perched on the top of a tree, and, failing to capture it by any other means, finally shot it. From the fragments he decided that the species was entirely unknown to science, and he forth- with fitted out an expedition at great cost to go in search of the insects. Two members of the party fell victims to the Papuan cannibals and another was rescued only in the nick of time. In spite of this unhappy commencement to his enter- prise, however, the naturalist persevered and ultimately succeeded in obtaining perfect specimens.
