div.head: ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS. THE SHADES OF A GREAT ENGLISHMAN.
div.p: ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS. THE SHADES OF A GREAT ENGLISHMAN.
JOHNSON'S HONE IN GOUGH SQUARE

Boswell's great biography has made Dr. Johnson immortal in English literature, and there is no likelihood that his memory will ever fade. That his writings would have secured immortality is doubtful in the last degree, but he lives in the pages of Boswell as a man of supreme human interest. He was a scholar, a writer and an Englishman— in many respects a typical one—but above all other things he was what Drummond called a "great human" and therein lies the everlasting charm. Mr. Cecil Harmsworth has earned the lively gratitude of every lover of English literature by purchasing and presenting to the nation the best relic that remains of Dr. Samuel Johnson. In Gough Court a few paces from Fleet street, the old house still remains in which he lived and toiled. Long forsaken as places of residence the courts off Fleet-street vibrate to the hum of printing presses, and the base- ment of Johnson's house has held machinery for several years. Lest the old walls should come asunder under the trembling of the printing press it was proposed to demolish them and build a firmer structure, but a better thing has happened. Clamorous news- paperdom is to be pushed from this sacred spot and the house, restored to its ancient aspect, is to be kept as a State possession where the shade of the great scholar, if he be 80 minded, can revisit the death-bed of his
DR. JOHNSON'S HOU&

wife, recall the death of his mother and the " Rasselas" written there to defray the cost of the funeral, and live over again the weary days when that great Dictionary was dragged to completion. But the thought of that Dictionary must surely be enough to keep away the spirit of the departed and one doubts whether Gough Square will ever be visited by the great shade of Johnson. Here, aided by six assistants who sat in the garret, he filled some toilsome years. The great work had been begun before he took up residence here, but it was the garret of Gough Square that witnessed the real labour. It was published on April 15th, 1755 at the price of DI 10s. and the world stood in awe at the achieve- ment. Johnson's preface is an admirable piece of writing, morbid perhaps and exaggerated, but historic as revealing the sense of burden under which he had groaned. " I may surely "he wrote" be contented without the praise of perfection, which if I could obtain in this gloom of solitude what would it avail me? I have protracted my work till most of those whom I wished to please have sunk into the grave."
_l'rorn T. P.'e Weekly.
SE IN GOUGH SQUARE.

apprehensions, live unrewarded and die unpitied, and who have been exposed to insult without a defender, and to censure without an apologist." The fact that they came and continJed to come is eloquent of what they found behind the rugged exterior of the great lexico- grapher. Like Goldsmith, Samuel Johnson had always a heart of pity for the distressed. THE BIRTH-PLACE OF THE "RAMBLER."

Gough Square was also the birth-place of the "Rambler "—a series of essays famous in literature, issued twice weekly and in the style of Addison's "Spectator." For two years Johnson wrote two essays a week, which sold at twopence and found about 500 Ipurchasers. Scornful ones declared that he I crowded them with big words so as to make his dictionary a necessity. He retorted in the pages of the " Idler" (also issued from Gough Square), that "words are hard only to those who do not understand them, and the critic ought always to inquire whether he is incommoded by the fault of the writer or his own. Every author does not write for every reader." Another literary task that engaged Johnson in the Gough Square days was his "Annotated Shakespeare." He had long cherished the idea, and in 1756, now that the Dictionary was launched, he took it up in earnest. Before a line was written he issued a prospectus which announced that the volumes would be ready for Christmas of the following year. Nine full years elapsed, alas, before they saw the light. Subscriptions had flowed in but the work dragged. It is doubtful whether he would ever have com- pleted it had rot Churchill stung him with a bitter satire; He for subscribers bates his book, And takes your cash ; bet where's the book ? No matter where ; wise fear, your know, Forbids the robbing of a foe ; ' But what, to serve our private ends, Forbids the cheating of our friends , ' The plain truth was that Johnson had undertaken the task out of need of money.

It was irksome and it was long, and must have cost him untold irritation during the I nine years through whichit dragged its weary course. We wonder how many people know that" Annotated Shakespeare" to-day.

div.head: JOHNSON'S DOMF.NTIC LIFE.
div.p: JOHNSON'S DOMF.NTIC LIFE.

One wonders what effect the Dictionary had upon the domestic life of Gough Square for Mrs. Johnson was hardly the woman to enjoy the passing up and down her pretty staircase of half a dozen hired clerks. Johnson in his own style, said that his wife was one who " desired the praise of neatness in her dress and furniture, as many ladies do, till they become troublesome to their best friends, slaves to their own besoms, and only sigh for the hour of sweeping their husbands out of the house as dirt and lumber." But the doctor was a master of grandiloquent exaggeration and we may take his summing up of " Tettie " with more than the usual grain of salt. That she longed to sweep out the litter of countless papers, may be taken as certain, and if the verbose doctor sat as long over his tea cup as Boswell avers, the application of the bosom to her husband would hardly have been a mistake. Mrs. Piozzi asked him in later years if he ever disputed with his wife. "Perpetually," he answered. And did he ever" huff" his wife? she ventured. "So often," said Johnson, 'that at last she called to me and said, ' Nay, hold, Mr. Johnson, and do not makes farce thanking God for a dinner which in a few minutes you will protest is not eatable.'" Yet these two were attached to each other and when her coffin was carried down the steps he said a fervent prayer that she might in spirit still inhabit the house and be with him to influence him in his dreams.

div.p: A CURIOUS HOUSEHOLD.

, Two weektitaei-the-ina-e-Will-Jr. Johnson took into his household Francis Barber, a negro, the first of a number of quaint figures who were to adorn it. Macaulay says that " a crowd of wretched creatures who could find no other asylum" sheltered here, but this is far from a correct statement. It is true, however, that Johnson's household was a strange one. One Robert Levet, an apothe-

div.head: RASELLAS.
div.p: RASELLAS.

The last task uilTe-ita;ii. in Gough-square is the one to which so much of tender memory clings. During the last year of his residence there his mother died. He was then issuing the " Idler " as a weekly paper, and poured out his feelings in words of solemn beauty: " The last year, the last day, must come. It has come and is past. The life which made my own life pleasant is at an end, and the gates of death are shut upon my prospects." To pay for his mother's funeral he wrote his " Rasselas," a little work that is read in days when the dust gathers upon the ponderous tomes, which he considered his greatest works. A few months afterwards he disbanded his curious household, and for twenty-five years or so dwelt elsewhere. We are glad the Gough-square home is to be preserved to us.
Who could quietly have watched that home of wisdom and charity go down under the crowbar and pickaxe? A. M.

"Rafael," said Gretchen. "Speak, ma diem," said Simard. "Redeem your promise, dinner is finished. Tell the story of your disappearance. We are all dying of impatience." "And of a woman's fatal curiosity. eh?" The coffee was served, they poured the cog. nac into their cups, and fixed their eager eyes on the hero of the evening. "We are all ready," was Chinnery's re- minder. "It was horribly dark and lonely in that in. fernal cage." mu. her? been there," exclaimed Gret,hen unthinking. "Ma chbre, so do I." Thin remark of Simard' net the other laughing; the Leopar- dess pouted, then joined in the laugh against herself.

. ...... "Those inexorable bars made me feel like a beast is a cage momentarily expecting to be slaughtered," Simard went on. "It must have been awful, dear old Asp, and we were jolly glad to find you still alive," said Blandford.
"Twice you have saved my life—chance again," said Simard. If I had not had the luck to tumble in the river we should be strangers now. Mon and, do you see? Chance; not skill."
"After you quitted my house, where did you go? What became of you?" said Gret- chen.

"My Gretchen, I wan thinking of you, and of the face that flashed pant when we were drinking to your beauty. The glimrde was of the slightest, but I was uneasy, because it was a face I well knew; yet there was a differ- ence. I was thinking of you, ma chere. of the face, and of the Princess. Her sufferings were in my heart, and I felt that I would re- joice to give happiness back to her. Suddenly, very suddenly, I was enveloped in a rug, n looped rope slipped over my shoulders, secured my arms. I could not struggle int about; I was like a trussed foal." . . .
Caught napping, Simard, enrol Bland. ford.

---"The weasel was asleep," chaffed Parlotte. And got his eyebrows shaved for his pains," grinned Chumery. "You laugh at me. I deserve it. They bore me away quick, ugh! The suffocation was not pleasant. The state of my mind when the rug was removed is difficult to de. scribe; my captors fled before I could catch them, or I would have punched their bends. When I saw the trap—rat trap—my courage rose; my indignation gave place to a very different feeling. Then I collected myself and prepared for the worst. Bela., my revolver had been lost or stolen from my pocket; I was defenceless. I was molested in the horrid wooden pen, and I laugh a little, just a little, because I knew my friends would search the city till they found the lost man. And if they did not fled him Himard would die hard. And so I slept on the straw till the morning." Lawson had not until then asked after the diamond necklace; now was Iris opportunity. "The diamonds—"

Stolen by that thief. But they will be yours again. I have only to fire the train, and he go up bang. See? Ila, ha, I shall not let the rascal get the laugh of me. The morning came, but I saw nothing; not a sound. I wrench at the wooden bars; they were stout, they would not more. Then I re- membered the monkeys in the Jardin trAc- climatation, and then I laughed again. But I did not laugh long, for I aaw pressed ngainst the bars the face of the biggest scoundrel wile ever escaped tho guillotine or your English galloun. In the bad light, with no beard, and his moustache shaved off. I did not recognise him. But when he spoke the voice pierced me like a detger -it was the voice of Victor Pirelli, the internees villain I had sworn one day to kill." "What did he any?" naked Lawnon. . .
Nine jute erdn, Give up the necklace and you are free.'" "And you?" _
"F;',- hie;; what could I say? I shruggod my shoulders, and said quite politely : ' And itlielit s ''T.'" t slied his hearers breath- lessly: -

"Then he came in the cage." "Two monkeys instead of ono," laughed Partette. "Yes, two, and one of them with murder in his eyes. We stood a few paces from each other preparing for the fight, end then he say in very formal tones, "Monsieur Simard, alias Simeon, I don't wish you any harm, but you have that which belongs to me. Don't foolishly resist. Yield gracefully; acknow- ledge your defeat." I will fight. Monsieur,' I said.' ' I am not defeated ; only at a disad- vantage.' Then he whistled, and brought three other men. The odds were great, and we fought and fought." "My poor Simard," said Gretchen, press. lag his hand. "Yes, me ohbre, your poor Simnrd was flung on the straw, a rag was forced in his mouth, something wet was laid on his face —Saere! I could not breathe • it was dark, very dark. I seemed to be falling into space, and after that there W. nothing till I woke and saw the face I love bending over the bed on which I slept." Simard folded his gums, waiting for hie guests to digeet the story. "I went on a foraging expedition yester- day," said Chinnery, "and roaming about old Paris I encountered the chiffonier who was the direct menss of our rescuing you from that dismal cage." Simard and Gretchen slightly shuddered at the recollection. "The pollee, while raiding the house, ar. rested th% owner and four of his satellites in a cellar. The poor devil who ventured to stop ne in the passage was discovered in the cage. Ids head swathed in bandages. I did hit rather hard, and this stick is not exactly a rattan," said Chinnery, polishing the stout oak club with his handkerchief. "Thus chance has succeeded in dispersing a gang of thieves, where the skill and experi- ence of the police failed," put in Simard. "How did you become possessed of this?" asked Blandford.
"I canno-t—expirtin," said Simeon, taking Count Rodrigues's trick dagger from Bland- ford.
"Whore did you find it?" "Clenched between your fingers, when yon were undretcted."

Simard pressed the spring and the keen blade darted from its sheath. After a care- ful examination he drew from a pocket-book a piece of steel, and joined the broken parts together. .My poor Alphonse, you sh II be avenged." said he, in a tone whose vib.-ant feeling cast • depression on those who understood the meaning of this display of sentiment. The evening of the carnival was ending in melan- choly. Simard had a man's dislike for any open display of weakness, and averted his head that he might hide the team which had sprung to his eyes. "I'll wire information to Scotland Yard," he continued presently, his voice shaking with emotion.

"But why, Rafael, indulge in thoughts of vengeance. Alphonse cannot be restored to life," said Gretchen, in her most melodious and persuasive tones. "An eye for an eye." His sternness was so unexpected that his guests for the soul of them could not speak. . . . . .
"Do not fight your Wiles over again." the woman pleaded. " Forget and forgive." In tones tender and full, he replied "Only fools forget and forgive, the wise never. I have spoken. Let us go."

div.p: A MYSTERY OF MAYFAIR,

CHAPTER XXVIII. stßsom's IMPRISONMENT.

The any City was not at its best, an op- press i e heat wave tilled the tables outside the cafes and restaurants to overflowing with exhausted and thirsty customers, while the popular boulevards and avenues were oom- pahtively deserted by the fashionable crowds of loungers. As for the general traffic, it be- came thinner and thinner as the evening wore on. Near the bridges the sweltering atmosphere was inten:illed by a mist float- ing upward from the river. A solitary fliers was rumbling over the uneven road of the Faubourg St. Antoine. Antoine Par- lotte put his head from the window and or- dered the driver to strop. Blandford and Chinnerv, disguised in travelling caps and tourist tweeds, alighted and strolled on- wards, the vehicle following at a snail's pace. " Are you sure you've not mistaken the spot?" asked Gretchen, who had insisted upon accompanying the men upon what the jeweller declared was an expedition of im- probabilities. "No. I'm positive," said Parlotte, throw- ing himself back on the seat of the ram- shackle cab and looking with his ope eye from the box window and reporting progress to the Leopardess, who was torn by anxiety and apprehension, an icy fear at her heart, that her "dear little man' had been done to death. "Hark !" said Gretchen.

A-1;;Tgillao-uTiTig-W,-;e1:;:as striking the hoar of ten, and than and not till than did Bland- ford and Captain Archer join them near to the Cafe St. Louis. They saw by the exterior the dusty windows and the dirty tawdry cur- tame and blinds, that the cafe was the re- sort of the lowest and most dangerous classes. They were prepared for a trap. Chinnerv, for preference, carried a heavy oaken !dick, and Blandford had chosen a boating crop. Firearms they had decided not to employ. At the last stroke of the hour, a man, ap- parently blind, came from a cul-de-sac, beat- ing the stone pavement with an iron shod @tick. fle passed and repassed the two men, repeating in a sing-song voice, "Pity the poor .blind." Blandford thought this beggar might be his shabby friend of tho morning, and ac- costed him, recognising the nasal whine of the chiffonier.

" Are you blind?" asked he suspiciously. "St. James's," ha murmured in his ear. The vagabond opened his eyes and smiled. "Did Waienr give me a franc thin mora- ine" he asked. "'I did," 'Sandford replied. " Where?"

...._._ . " Under the archway of the Hotel St. James's. I was seated in a motor." "You are a comrade of Waieu Simeon?" The vagrant's frightened whisper could hardly be heord. "I am," said Blandford. "And would save him"

"From whom and (rein what?" dnianded Alec, putting the crook handle of his crop at the bark of the man's neck and thus pre- venting him from moving away. The vag- rant cast a searoliing glance at the cafe win- dow and said in a shaky voico, "From slow death."

_ . "Bo explicit, if you can." "kUsieu, there is but five minutes. fie is • prisoner in an adjoining house. Madame of the cafe sent me. Come." "Shall we trust this beggar?" said Chin- eery to Blandford. "There is no other way that I can see," Blandford replied. Chinnery ran to the cab, spoke a few wortis of encouragement to the Leopardeis and joined Blandford and his guide, who led them along a dimly lighted passage. A door in the centre was partly opened, showing the interior of the cafe. A rapid survey was. suMcient. There were seated at the tables the usual elements of riot, insnrrection, pil- lage, and murder. A stout woman stood by the door, which she closed while speaking to their guide. "Au troisieme," she said, and she was go

-Step softly, M'sieurs," said the rag. picker, conducting them through a narrow subway, up a flight of slippery worn step, re- minding the two men of Gretchen'. dream. They were in a house a few yards from the cafe. Silence was impressed upon them, and at the bottom of • staircase they waited for their conductor to light • small lantern. There was not a sound, the stillness was deadly, it weighed upon the men like lead. The ahaded candle held aloft flickered, but Blandford and Chinnery saw enough, and their misgivings increased; the success of their enterprise seemed remote. The two friends had an uneasy, creepy sensation, which culminated into a feeling of horror when a door on the top floor was unlocked and thrown open. "Faugh!" they both exclaimed, disgusted at the foul fumes pouring from the room. En- tering, they started back, aghast at the sight which met their eyes. The apartment was of considerable dimensions; in the middle was erected a cage of strong wooden bars. On a bundle of straw lay the detective asleep, or in a stupor. There was the glassy stare of death in the open eyes, but his chest rising and falling regularly proved they had not come too late. Evidently, he was under tho Influence of some narcotic, probably morphia or chloral. The vagrant unlocked and pushed up the small wicket, under which they crawled. Blandford and Chinnery lifted Simeon in their arms and bore him from the den, urged on to speed by their guide. They were ap- proaching the door in the passage when a ruf- fianly man staggered from the café and barred further progress. Fortunately, the door closed automatically, or the glare of light would have betrayed the three men standing breathlessly waiting. They could only stand quiet till the fellow discovered them, and when he did no, Chinnery's hood clasped his throat. "Run for the cab, Alec; I'll settle this ran-

cal,and join you -hair on." The netting sun was casting lengthening shadows on the tables in the garden. of the Alcamr. Very merry were the young and the middle-aged, for the dinner wee above re- proach, the wins exhilirating, and the cool- neon of the night sir refreshing to the heated bodies of those whom mission in life for the tooineni. vim that of amusing themselves. ' ' '

?he light shed from a ha; hanging over a table in • secluded portion of the grounds re- vealed the faces of Parlotte, Blandtord, Chin- wry, Lawson, Mlle. Ranee, and Simeon, who looked none the worse for his imprisonment. The careful nursing of the lady had restored him to his usual state of robust health, and there he sat, his wit and vivaciousness infect- ing all his guests with gaiety. "Perlotte and I are disputing as to whether chance or skill serves the detecti ,o best," said Blandford, speaking to Simard, who had discarded his alias, Simeon, for his legiti- mate name. . .

The ex-detective answered alowly and re- fiectively : "Skill and experience have their wales and go far, but chance is the greatest factor, chance is a flirt, her favours aro few; yet she wins the game where skill often fails. Chance, mon ami, lured me to Marlow. Chance revealed that my charming Mdlle. Guthrie and Mdlle. 'rrafford were one end the same person, and it was chance threw me amongst the comrade. who are with no to- night„ my honoured guests." 111 trouble you for five francs, Monsieur Blandford," said the chuckling Parlotte. "Simard has decided our bet of chance against skill."

div.p: CHAPTER XXIX. PRINCIIBB KOLA KOWSK

Lawson and Simard were wandering about the gardens of the Tuileries deep in confiden- tial conversation. This delightful reboil of the l'arisians was nearly empty, and there- fore they had no occasion to seek for more secluded quarters. Simard was turning over in his mind the incidents that had occurred at Marlow, between Miss Trafford, Aide, Niggins, and Lawson. That Lawson was or could be a child ef the harem, the ex-detee- tire resolutely declined to believe. lie medi- tatively broke a biselfit, scattering the frog- ' meats on the pathway for the benefit of the ! birds flocking at his feet. "Mon aspi. kir& ere, like Rep; the/ tr.apple

on the weak. - see how teat tag pigeon gobbles up everything, leaving the rest tq starve. Be brave, look the world in the face, care for no man. There are halting places in our lives when we have to take a choice of one of two roads. The right and the wrong. To brave hearts nothing is impossible. If by chance you take the wrong load, travel back and seek the right. See? That is what you call logic, mon nisi. Miss Trafford declares that you, Michael Law,on, are the son of • slave. The lady lies', she dodges the ques- tion when you ask for proof. Simard is a wizard and can read the horoscope of Michael Lawson. Shall I reveal the secret that the twinkling stars 'eve 'idden?" " You are striving to soften in, humilia- tion," said Lamson in a choking voice. "Mai., Comment? I will sweep the cross- ing for you, what the English call 'paving the way. Your tread is sure and your shoes must not be splashed with mud. Suppose you are--a—mistake, you are the same as others, flesh and blood, always the tame dear comrade." . .

" Happiness, complete happiness is unob- tainable, ' said Lawson, not convinced "Then Blandford and Captain Chinnery may not think mo worthy et their regard.' "They are English rntlemen, and when I sa• that, yon 'avo your answer." '"The world is censorious." "And filled with good fellows, moo anti," said the jolly little Frenchman. Lawton 's dark ascetic face lost much of its sadness, and he bluntly spoke of his birth to Simard, who said with a dry chuckle ac- companying his speech: "Figure to yourself that I am a 'arliquin. I strike- Michael Law- son with my wand, and, rresto ! there is another man. See?"

Lawson turned his head away and sighed profoundly. " Cheer up, cheer up," said Simard in a voice of encouragement. "Ch.' up, the good time is coming. Cheer up. My skill is not at fault. Simnrd will prove that von were born of great and noble parents. Lift up your eyes and stare at the sun—you need not blush." . . . .

"Do not encourage false hopes. I feat the worst. For myself, I can bear the ills of fortune. But for the girl I love it is hor- rible. A man works and forgets in the ex- citement of toil the indignities which have been thrust on him. But for a young and lovely woman—" Here for the life of him he could not restrain his emotion. " Why she is a mark for the libertine, and the scorn of her own sex. Prove that we, that she and I are not the sport of cruel fate, sad all that I possess is yours." Had Lawson studied how to press Simard into his service, he could not have employed a more convincing argument. The French- man had no thought of money, but of his niece's untimely death, and he there and then registered a vow to assist his friend to the utmost. But he must respect the cenfi- dance reposed in hini by Mdlle. Runes. Her permission obtained, he would bring Michael and the Princess Kolakowski together. He longed to put his surmises and deductions to the test, to prove that they were indisput- able facts and not merely Eastern fairy tales.

"Think not of Mademoiselle Aide an a tin- ter, think of her rather an your fiancée. Be content for the present, bask in the warmth of love's bright flame. Think, mon and, of the happy day when you will be hound to each other for life and death, for better or worse. Think of the proud moment when you place the famous necklace about her slender neck."
"Simard, Simard, don't tantalise me by such a dream," LaWAMI cried, in a tome of nhllo,Pant But what must be, will be; It is ordained."
-;;71- would fain banish memory. Let us walk on," said Lawson. _ .
.."Bani;4ll memory! When your heart is en, chained?" urged Simard. "Lout, Simard, lost, like the. necklace." . _
"But—lo be hidebts." regainki. The villain pay s
"Still hankering after revenge?" "Revenge? No—l only wont justice.
"neve uyou thought Of the .discloeuree it will bring about. Of the innocent people who will be compelled to give their evidence et

"True. But Signor Victor Parretti mu,' suffer the penalty of his crime," said Simern stubbornly. "A trial in open court. Sen- tence and the hangman. He murdered Al- phonse, shot my niece's lover, and broke the poor child's htert." "Offer him a choice of roads." "To eternity?" "Ay, this. An Eastern remedy." Lawson's manner of speech was peculiar, It conveyed so much that Simard's keen eyes dwelt on him apprehensively, and he almost snatched from his fingers a tiny phial no larger than a thimble. "A drop of that on the tongue, then good- bye—no more trouble, no more trials—ne hanging. He could choose his own road, at least give him a choice. Are you resolved?"

" I -am. Such men are a nurse. Think of those gone before, of homes destroyed, women ruined. Think of those. If I spare him, he will still commit crimes. No, I will not spare him even for you, my friend. My patience shall be untiring till he lies there," stamping his heel on the ground—"in tho grave that he has dug for himself." "Vengeance is mine; I will repay," quoted Lawson.
-lii-F;" coughed Simard. "You are taking a thorny path.* "Which such as I mast travel." "Once set the law in motion and none can foretell where it will roll," said Lawson,

from publicity. "We will be happy this morning," said Simard, accompanying his words by a leindly pat on the young maa's shoulder. "Clear my dishonoured name," said Law- son. "Leave revenge alone." "Ali, that is another affair altogether," said Simard, and then with a word of adieu, he strolled away that he might keep an ap- pointment with Gretchen Runes at the Louvre.

The Princess Kolakowski wan Rented before a eheval-glass, in a tastefully furnished dres- siug-room of small dimensions in Millie. Enoch' apartment. Her hair was loose and fell over her shoulders in soft wavy masses, forming a frame which set off her somewhat sad face. The tresses, which Gretchen was brushing, once of a golden hue, were thickly sprinkled with grey, yet they were still luxuriously long and thick. She still re- tained traces of former loveliness and looked what she was, a woman of noble birth. Her broad brow was of the intellectual type, and none could mistake the order to which she belonged. Her fifty. The settled melaneholy in her eyes en- hanced the Interest that her pessonality aroused, and her amiability endeared her equally to those who served her and those who claimed her friendship. Mdlle. Runes bad usually a qnite remarkable flow of con- versation, but this morning she was inex- plicably reserved, and vaguely apprehensive of the result M the surprise planned by Simard and herself while in the galleries of the Louvre. She did not doge say a word, and yet she was longing to tell all' the truth to this poor girl who had suffered, her health undermined, and her brain weakened by the loss of husband and children. A sigh of fatigue escaped the Prince., she missed the lively gossip of her friend and fell into a train of melancholy thoughts of her husband around whose memory she bad woven a halo of tittered romance. Gretchen having com- pleted her self-imposed duties, which she claimed its her particular pri, liege, became more worried. She had at that moment & dull end hopeless feeling of failure, and yet she must prepare the Prioress for Simar& and Layrson'e approaching visit. There come at bud, after a long hesitation. n swift impul- sive decieion, and she rose abruptly from her chair, tidied the dressing-table, and opened her mouth to begin. She could not however at once attract the attention of Felicia, whose eves were mournfully regarding her own reflection in the glass. her brows were knit, her lips compressed, she teas recalling those days of turmoil which, had caused her exile and the mysterious disappearance of the one man in all the world of whom she had been inordinately fond. Then the memory of Trafford Khan seemed to rise up and peer over her shoulder, and with • flash of almost, mad terror, she closed her eyes, clasping the hand of the arm encircling her neck. Gretchen affectionately kissed her, and presently she recovered her usual composure. Then she rose and passed from her dressing. gam beto the boudoir adioinies. where the

two old friends sat down updir a couch to- gether. " I am growing old, Gretchen," said the Princess. ' My glass is no flatterer, and • recluse is hut a dull companion for you, who aro so gay, while I am only a clog on your vivacity. My Gretchen, I have a longing for peace, a rest from brooding. Oh, my be- loved," she said pitifully, "I want you, I shall always want you, and we are separated for ever. I wonder," she said more calmly, "if my children are alive?" " Living in Persia perhaps, ignorant of their parentage—Trafford Khan, hateful wretch, shall be compelled to disclose where they are. A gertleman upon whom I ran rely has undertaken, for my sake, to trace your children," Gretchen flashed at the look of surprise on the face of the Princess. " I will offer him half of my possessions," she cried._ .

"Nay, he would not accept a single son. Be consoled by tho thought that in every life, however dark, there may at any time creep in a ray of light." OIL, would that I could share Tour faith, dear Gretchen. No light can cast its rays on me. I have lived among the shadows too long." Gretchen shut her ears and would not listen to more ill the same strain, she was striving for a way to prepare the Princess for the test insisted on by Simard—the bring- ing of Lawson unannounced into her pre- sence.

patient," Raid Gretchen. " Patient! Ask God if I have not been patient," she cried, in tones of anguish, lift- ing her face from her hands and looking re- proachfully at her friend. "If the Prince was banished to Siberia, these is a chance of his having escaped. ' " He is dead. Gretchen, all efforts are vain; intuition tells me so."
But his.-;;on--Ilv7i; is living " "Why do you believe that?" "Because the Khan had no object in con- cealing his death." . . . .

tttttt eyes met. What a story each silently told the other. Gretchen's lays was grave, for the plan might fail. Felicia's character hail never been remarkable for buoyancy, her early training hail been against that. But her love for Sergius had roused all the warmth that was latent in her heart.

"Joy seldom kills and maternal joy never, at least I trust not," thought Gretchen, re she saw the hands of the clock pointing to the hour at which Simard had arranged to omit her. They were both filled with a spirit of unrest and no began to wander up and down the room. Their walk was a poem of motion as they kept pace for pace, aurrepti. Homily scrutinising each other', countenance, anxiously listening, and their feverish eyes glancing at the white and dusty road. "She suspects there ía anmething afoot, something in the wind, but I dare not speak," Gretchen 'a thought!: ran. "I do wish they would come," she muttered, loosening the lace at her throat, for the tightness increased her irritation ; but though agitated she was far too accomplished a woman of the world to allow her feelings to gain ascendancy over a solf.imposed duty. "Dear Felicia," she began, "a few even- ings ago, I was introduced by Parlotte to Monsieur Rafael Simard, a man of singular intelligence and integrity. He in partly ac- quainted with your fatntly. history."
"Can you rely on gis dise'retionr es. claimed the. Princess in confused alarm. . . . _ .
"Absolutely," maid Gret.hen firmly. "Ile may be bribed--" . . .

"My dear Felicia, Monnieur Siniard is not a Bosnian. Bribe him! He is above paltry treachery." Gretchen's active zeal on be- half of a atranger surprised the Prince and she said thoughtfully: "This is the only time I can remember your defending any kind of man. Who is the gentleman? And why do you take so much intermit in Ids acquaintance of a few hours?" Seeing the blush mantling Mlle. Rune's face, she maid jealously, "Hero I a rival in your regard?" "No, Felicia, you gain two adherents in- stead of one."
"And his position? "lie is of no occupation." Gretchen re. trained from confiding Simard's antecedents to the Princess. " When shall I sec him?"

"I expect him eery minute. He begs an Interview with you, which I sincerely hope will bring you within view of peace." An interruption occurred in the shape of a servant announcing, "Monsieur Rafael bimard." _ . _

div.head: _ THE COST AND LOSS OF DRINKING,
div.p: _ THE COST AND LOSS OF DRINKING,

Sir Thomas Whittaker, M.P., has an article in a recent issue of "Omen's" on the Cost and Loss of Drinking. Ile estimates that the t xpenditure on intoxicants during the last five years has averaged about A:165,000,000. Dalacting I:35,000,000 as the average amount received during that time by the State from the Trade in the form of duties on liquor and licence., the direct coat of the liquor to the public is £130,000,000 a year. Then there is the indirect coat —the cost of the poverty, crime, insanity, and disease caused by drink, together with the !OM of the pro- ductive labour of those who are thus incapacitated The indirect loss, Mr. Whittaker thinks, balances the revenue which the State derives from the trade, no he puts the expenditure on drink down at £165,000,000 a year.

div.head: FREE OF ALL TAXES.
div.p: FREE OF ALL TAXES.

Considering for a moment what this £165,000,000 a year means Mr. Whittaker points out that the ' estimsted tax revenue for the current year was £142,455,000, and nays that sere the' money spent on drink devoted to meeting national expenditure we should be free of all taxes. "The housing problem is • preening one, but few people realise that we spend as much on drink every yearns is the annual value of every dwelling house in the United Kingdom. That is to nay, the money spent on drink would suffice to enable the whole nation to live rent free."

div.head: SOME COMPARISONS.
div.p: SOME COMPARISONS.

" We hear much at times of railway fares and rates, and the cost cf transit and communication," Mr. Whittaker goes on to state, "bat do we realise that !we spend enormously more on dunk than all our railways take for passenger, goods, mineral, cattle, and parcel traffic, for all they do and every service they render? The amount of the drum bill would pay the cost of everybody and everything which is now carried by rail, and, and leave a large balance to pay for those who would wish to travel and the goods which would be sent if they could be carried free of charge." Mr. Whittaker also states that the money spent on drink is greater than the unimproved annual value of the whole of the land of the country, whether built on or not.

THE FAMILY HANDICAP. PAREN IS BARRED FROM A WIDNES APPOINTMENT.

A epecial meeting of the Widnes Council Iras held on Monday to confirm the resolution of the General Purpose. Committee that, out of 332 applicants, Mr. II Colton be appointad Town Hall keeper aud Mayor's attendant. . . . .
At the previous council meeting it had been decided that the position be advertised, and that the words "no encumbrance "be struck net. . . . . . .

Alderman Neil, moving the adoption of the minutes said tee committee bad knocked out all applicant', who had ,ny family because of the lock of accommodation at the Town Hall. The age was fixed from 55 to 45, and the salary was fixed at E 2 ss. the officer to provide all cleaning materials. Councillor liampson described as most unfair the ban place upon a man and wife who had one or two children. Instead of barring a man with one or two children, the council ought to assiet them. The appointment wan confirmed by It votes to 5. RUNCORN PARENTS NEGLECT.

At Runcorn on Saturdey, Albert Ravenscroft, of Regent-street, and Emily Revenscroft, his wife, were summoned for neglecting their five children. Superin- tendent Emden said the five children were at the police station at half-iast ten cn Monday night and told him they had no tea that day. There man no food ,in tha house. Eavenscroft played the piano in public. houses at tie week.and. There were two previous convictions for child neglect ageirst him and nine for failing to send toe children to school. Revenscrolt (who is well connected) was sent to gaol for three months sml Lis wife for six weeks.

A distreasiog fatality to a little boy, three 3 ears old, happened on Tuesday night at Sutton, St. Helena Some children were swinging from iron railings which surmout.t a low wall near Harriaon-street, when the stonework gave way, and the railing, fell spun the children. James Lee, of 6, Harrison-street, was taken to the St. Helens Hospital, and died ten minutes after. ward,. LORD ROLMER ON SOCIALISM AND TYRANNY.

Speckles on the Trade Unions Bill in the House of Commons on need., Lord Weimer, while recogniaing that some legislation was necessary, said the situation before the Osborne judgment was nothing short of • hideous Manny. The trade unionists claimed that in the more highly organised trt.des all working men must join the unions, and that, having joined, they roust pay • levy towards the upkeep of Socialism in the iluane of Common.. During the past five or six years many thou- ..da of men had left the Lancashire end Chtshi re hl iners' Federation because of the political complexion thrown over the trade union movement by the advent of the Socialist Labour party. The federation had become alarmed, and were now forcing men to join by method more brutal than theee of a German drill a This bill would enable them to force the. men to con- tribute towards the support of political principles; which they abominated. It was idle to nay the Labour party wee primarily a trade union party and not a political party, when they found that ontly all its members were Socialists, Homo Rulers and seculeriats. div.head: VERY REV. J. P. WHITTLE, 0.8.13.
div.p: VERY REV. J. P. WHITTLE, 0.8.13.

THE CLERGY OF ST. ALBAN'S (R.C.) CHURCH. The church of St. Alban, Bewsey-street, is the mother church of the Roman Catholics in Warrington and since its erection in 1823 it has been the centre of unremitting and successful effort under the direc- tion of devoted priests who have had the loyal and self-srcrificing support of a faithful congregation. The first available record of Roman Catholicmm in Warrington, subsequent to the Reformation, goes back to the time n hen Charles Ist was beheaded. Mass used to he celebrated at a moated grange about three miles south of Wadley, near Wigan, and worshippers from Warrington walked over to attend. A Lout 1700 • temporary place of worship was found in a are- house in Foundry-street, Warrington, aml many years afterwards, in 1771, Father Bennet Shuttleworth came to the town with permission to establish a mission. A number of different places were used in succession as chapels—amongst them a room in the old "Feathers inn," Friars Gate ; a large hall in Dallam-lane, afterwards used as a Methodist Chapel ; a room of Aahton's, in Sankey-street ; and a room behind the " Cooper's Arms, Bewsey-street. Father Shuttlewot th lived till 1774, and hi. successor Father Anaeltu Bradshaw placed the mission van per- manent basis by building a church in 1778. This building is the present League of the Cross Hall in Bewsey-street. This church had to serve the need. of Warrington Roman Catholics for about 40 years. Father Alolyneux, 0.5.11., then built a new church and presbytery, the present St. Alban's which was opened in 1823.
The prrsent rector of St. Alban's, the Very Rev. John Placid Whittle, O.S.R , cornea of an old

Lancastrian Roman Catholic family which suffered much for the Faith during the days of the Penal Laws. Ile was born at Brownedge, Dear Preat n, on June 27th, 1838, rind is therefore nearly 73. At the age of twelve he was sent to Ampleforth Collette situated in the beautiful Vale of Mowbray about 20 mih e from York. At one time it w.ts expected he would be articled to his uncle, who was a ' '

lawyer, hut from an early age his own inclina- tions turned towards the priesthood. After a complete course of classics and philosophy he entered the Benedictine Order at Ampleforth in 18.58. Immediately after his novitiate he heroine a teacher of clas,ics at the College, where he remained till 1809, when he came to.St„..Alban's, (then the only Roman

Catholic Church in Warrington) to supply for Father Hall who had a three mouths' illness. Early in 1870 he was appointed curate at St. Alatv's,Liverpool, where he remained till September, 1873, when he was appointed Rector of St. Mary's, Woolton, near

Liverpool. During his seven years there he doubled the school accommodation, beautified the church, adding new eacribties and cloister, and cleared the church eta debt of £l,ot. In the year 1880 he was appointed Prior of Ampleforth, his old Alma Maier. At the end of his term of office in January 1884 he became Rector of S. Anne's, Edge Lverpool. During the years he remained there ,he built a new infant school, enlarged the church by removing the sanctuary which was square and providing a new,one apsidal shape, midi transepts and side chapels,and built a new Priory. In 1890 he came hack to St. Alban's, Wart ington. Since then all the old windows have been taken out and stained glass for the most part inserted and electric light installed

Al-out three prate ago Falb, Whittle kept his golden jubilee in religion, and it will doubtless be remembered how his people filled the Parr Hall ono evening, amongst the gathering being the Mayor of Warrington and a large contingent of fellow priests from all parts. A beautiful illuminated address was read and a purse of gold containing over £5OO presented. With that sum and other subscriptions he put a new porch and font to St. Alhan's and a very large west end window of choice stained glass. Father Whittle is deservedly beloved of his flock to vrhom he has ministered with untiring seal, and by his sj mpathy and willingness to help in all good won ks be has also gained the goodwill and esteem of people of all denominstiom. He haa always taken a keen interest and an active part in movements for the welfare of the town, and especially of the poor, and for foul teen years has been on the Committee of Management of the Infirmary.

Father Whittle has an earnest an I efficient colleague hi Father Philip Lawrence Buggies, 0.5.8. His early days were spent in Birmingham, where his father was a railway contractor. At the age of twelve—in 1890—Father Buggits , went to A mpleforth College. Yorkshire, and whilst a student at that famous institution he defi...itely decided to prepare himself for the priesthood. Join- ing the Benedictine Order at the Abbey in 1890, he went to Belmont Monaately, near Hereford, where he stay, d for Lug. years. In 1900 he returned to Ampleforth to teach, his principal subject being mathematics. Ile s; as ordained priest in 1904 by Bishop Lacey at kliddleebor ugh, and he is at present serving his first curacy at St. Alban* where he has been stationed since 1905. Ile is a very conscientious; worker and takes a special interest in the young men of the congregation.

Ihe children and choir acquitted themselves admirably, due in no small measure to the untiriog efforts of Mr. Frock Warn., who discharged the duties of trainer and organist. Is the morning the Her. Mr. New and his Critics. Sir,— After the delivery to your office of my pre- vitas letter the thought occurred to my mind that Mr. New was over-enthusiastic in his denunciation of Tariff Reform, awl did not intentionally " pander to the gallery." Mr. New's reply, however, encourages me to think differently. I have a distinct recollection of hearing Mr. Ni w use similar language to that con- tained in his letter, as well as the argument to which I drew his attention, and Ido not deny the accuracy of his statements. At the name time he tloes not deny having applied his argumente and statement of facts in such a manner and fur a purpose which is °Nen.- tionable to every fair-minded woman or man. I repeat, Sir, it is moat unfair to accuse individuals, be they Liberal or Tory, for having to resort to methals, however deplorable, for which the present capitalistic system and rot individuals r individual firms is solely responsib!e. My faits are quite in order, and I hope I have made my point clear this time. In conclusion I sincerely thank Mr. New for his advice, but an opportunity to tackle the speaker on the spot was not available during my short stay and I did not wish to rudely interrupt. Mr. New says " I am afraid he has allowed his Judgment to be some- what narrow." Let me assure Mr. New that nothing could be further from the truth, indeed I feel very proud of the fact that whenever and wherever I have had an oppott unity to speak on behalf of Socialism I have never vilified either Liberals or Tories butt have tried ii the best r f nip very humble abilities, to expose the fallacy of Liberalism and Toryism. The same cannot be aid of my Liberal friends; some of the Liberal tactics during the Orford Wald Elections of 1fi08.9 in which i I figured as an unsuccessful candi- date are still fresh in try meinory.—Yours sincerely, JAS. Teachers and the Coronation.

Sir,--In view of what was said at the Education Meeting ou Monday last, when the teachers were charged a,* want of sympathy and seltiAliness, we are instructed by the committee of the Warringbm Teachers' Association to put before your readers the real facts of the case, no that they may judge for them- selves as to what truth there is in the allegations made We wish to make quite clear that there was no proposal of any sort made by the Education Committee to the teachers; the proposal came from the Sub-Com- mittee of the Coronation Committee. This Sub- Committee drafted a scheme which was dangerous and extremely difficult, if not impossible of execution. The head teachers were summoned by the Mayor and asked to suggest details for car eying out the proposed scheme. They pointed cot the difficulties, lent were told they could not discuss the general plan. At a meeting f the bead teachers held subsequently, the difficulties of massing 14,000 children of all ages, from four to fourteen, inn remote park, difficult of access, having only one entrance, founded by a river, with little or no aanimry accommodation, appreaclied by a narrow, dangerous and crowded bridge, appeared insuperable. The head teachers requested the Mayor to call a sec, ad meeting. At this meeting the above difficulties were again pouted • at, and an alternative scheme, that the children should be assembled in four or more centres where they could be massed in safety and within remorable distance of their homes, was respectfully suggested. The members of the Core:nation Sub-Committee at once dropped the whole luminous. The resentment, if any, was entirely to their side, and upon them and them alone, must rest the responsibililly for the abandenun nt of the celebratiors as far as the children are concerned. We wish also to odd that practically every teach, r in Warricgton had volunteered, and, moreover, had signed an undertaking to do everything poisible to give the children a happy and memorable day, whichever scheme was adopted. And this was done a consider- able time before there was the least suggestion or thought of a week's holiday. In fact, it meant that the teachers were willing to surrender whit had been a holiday hit them for many years- the day before Walkirg Day- no that the children might have a joyous time. That is, the teachers were prepared to work, and to work hard on Coronation Day and Walking Day, when all the rest of the world was enjoying itself, and the results are chargr s of want of eympatby and selfiahnees.- Yours truly, JOHN W. PARKER, P,esident, FRANK 11, LONOSHAW, Secretary. Warrington and District Teachers' Association.

I should like to submit a few observatiot.s summarising the points. The first letter was a protest against the Cottrell Chamber being used for political propaganda. To this Miss Waring quotes Sir George Kemp who said "he believe!" at meshing or other. To this inadequate proof Mr. Beaumont again asks for at me specific charge discrediting the canvass. And what is Mine Waring's final reply' Simply thin the more he (Mr. Beaumont) talks about it the Letter for us." Could one ini•gine • more absurd answer? To a simple queathm bliss Waring rant give a definite affirmative or negative. Either the canvass referred to is right or it rong, and Miss Waring is asked to prove her statements discrediting the figures. Not being able to do no, 1 suppose the only way out of it is to ignore it. Here sir two pointy which bare come out clearly in the corryspondence and which emphasise the weak-

WARRINGTON ATHLETIC CLUB. MEMBERS' RACES.

A fair number of local sportsmen visited the ground of Crostields' Recreation Club, to witness one cycle and two flat handicaps, in which there was keen competition and , spirited finishes. The 300 yards was won by J. E. Cartwright from the brothers Sid- ' dall, who fought out a desperate finish with second place going to the Younger brother. The half mile cycle provided J. Ardern with an opportunity of annexing his first prize, and another novice, in H. Hough, fully: merited the minor honour of second place. The 1,000 yards brought out 29 starters, of whom a promising novice in G. Wake- field made the best possible use of his handicap allowance and won by a bare yard from the veteran, H. K. Jepson, who appears to be moving almost as well as ever. Details:--300vds. Final: 1, J. Cartwright 2, W. Siddall; 3, A. Siddall. 2 yards, inches. Time, 31 seconds. Half mile cycle final: Time, 314 seconds. Half mile cycle. Final: 1, J. Ardern, 65yds.; 2, H. Hough, 100vds; 3, C. Berry, scratch; 4, J. Deeley, 166vds. Won by a length, 20 yards, wheel.
